units.title: Work, Energy & Power
units.anchoring_phenomenon: A roller coaster car is pulled slowly to the top of the first hill — the tallest point on the track — and then released without any engine. It speeds through loops, valleys, and hills for the entire ride. Where does all that energy come from, and why does each successive hill have to be shorter than the first?
essential_questions: How do we quantify the energy transferred to or from an object by a force?
How is energy stored in a system, and what determines how much is stored?
How does the conservation of energy allow us to predict the motion of objects?
units.crse_theme: Students explore energy concepts through diverse cultural and historical lenses — the physics of traditional tools and simple machines across civilizations (Egyptian ramps, Incan terraces, West African pounding mortars), the contributions of James Prescott Joule and Emilie du Chatelet to our understanding of energy, and how access to energy resources connects to social justice and equity.

formative: Exit tickets on work and kinetic energy calculations
summative: Investigation: Conservation of Energy in a Spring-Mass System

investigations: Investigation 3: Conservation of Energy in a Spring-Mass System

lessons.title: Work as Energy Transfer
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can calculate the work done on an object by a force, including cases where the force is at an angle to the displacement.
lessons.circle_prompt: What does the word 'work' mean to you in everyday life? How might a physicist define 'work' differently? Think of a time you worked really hard physically — were you always moving something?
lessons.do_now: A student pushes a 10 kg box across the floor with 50 N of force for 3 meters. Another student holds a 10 kg box above their head for 30 seconds without moving. Who did more work in the physics sense? Explain your reasoning.
materials: Smooth surfaces and rough surfaces (cardboard, sandpaper)

engage.description: Display two images: (1) A person pushing a heavy box across a room. (2) A person holding a heavy box perfectly still above their head, sweating and straining. Ask: Who is doing more work? Students vote — most will say the person holding the box. Reveal that in physics, only the person pushing the box does work, because work requires displacement in the direction of the force.

explore.description: Groups use spring scales to pull a 1 kg mass across a table at constant speed over 1.0 m. They record the force and calculate W = Fd. Then they pull the same mass up a ramp (at an angle) to the same height and record the force and distance along the ramp. Students compare the work done in each case and discover that W = Fd cos(theta) accounts for the angle between force and displacement.

explain.description: Define work: W = Fd cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Units: Joules (J) = N·m. Key cases: theta = 0 degrees (force parallel to displacement, maximum work), theta = 90 degrees (force perpendicular, zero work — like carrying a box horizontally while gravity pulls down), theta = 180 degrees (force opposes displacement, negative work — like friction). Work through three practice problems: pushing a lawn mower at an angle, lifting a weight vertically, and friction slowing a sliding object.

elaborate.description: A 40 kg child pulls a 15 kg sled with a rope that makes a 30-degree angle with the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 40 N and the child pulls the sled 100 m. Students calculate the work done by the child on the sled, the work done by gravity, and the work done by the normal force.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 60 N force is applied to a box at 45 degrees above the horizontal. The box moves 8.0 m along the floor. Calculate the work done by the applied force. Then explain why the normal force does zero work.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a work calculation flowchart: Step 1 — Identify F and d. Step 2 — Find angle between F and d. Step 3 — Plug into W = Fd cos(theta). Include a cosine value reference card for common angles (0, 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees).
differentiation.on_level: Complete the spring scale exploration and all practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate work done by a variable force using the area under a Force vs. Displacement graph. Analyze the work done during the compression of a spring where force changes with position.
differentiation.ell: Provide visual diagrams showing force and displacement vectors with the angle clearly labeled for each problem. Use color-coding: blue arrow = force, red arrow = displacement, green arc = angle. Include bilingual vocabulary card.
differentiation.iep: Provide a W = Fd cos(theta) reference card with a diagram. Break multi-step problems into single calculations. Provide a calculator tutorial for the cosine function. Allow use of the common angles reference card on assessments.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Emilie du Chatelet, an 18th-century French physicist who demonstrated that energy is proportional to velocity squared (not just velocity), laying groundwork for the concept of kinetic energy. Despite her contributions, she was often overshadowed by her male contemporaries, including Voltaire.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'work': A person holding a heavy box above their head does zero work in physics because___. Both pushing and lifting require effort, but only one involves work when the box moves horizontally because___. The force was applied at an angle of 60 degrees to the displacement, so the work done was___.

vocabulary.definition: The energy transferred to or from an object by a force acting over a displacement; W = Fd cos(theta), measured in Joules
The SI unit of energy and work; 1 J = 1 N·m = 1 kg·m^2/s^2
Work done when the force component is in the same direction as the displacement, increasing the object's energy
Work done when the force component opposes the displacement, decreasing the object's energy (e.g., friction)
When the force is perpendicular to the displacement (cos 90 = 0) or when there is no displacement

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is Work? — The Physics Definition vs. Everyday Meaning
Section 2: Calculating Work — W = Fd cos(theta)
Section 3: Positive, Negative, and Zero Work
Section 4: Work Done by Multiple Forces

cer.phenomenon: A warehouse worker pushes a 50 kg crate 20 m across a smooth floor using 200 N of horizontal force. A second worker pushes an identical crate the same distance using 250 N of force directed 37 degrees below the horizontal. The second worker claims they did more work because they used more force.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the work equation, I claim that the first worker actually did more useful work on the crate because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the work done by each worker using W = Fd cos(theta). Compare the horizontal component of each worker's force.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because even though Worker 2 applied a larger force, the angle meant that only the ___ component contributed to moving the crate forward, resulting in W = ___ J compared to Worker 1's W = ___ J. This demonstrates why the angle in W = Fd cos(theta) matters.

lessons.title: Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can calculate kinetic energy using KE = 1/2 mv^2 and apply the work-energy theorem to relate net work to changes in kinetic energy.
lessons.circle_prompt: What makes something dangerous when it's moving fast — a car, a baseball, a bullet? Is it the speed alone, or does the mass matter too? Think of examples where a slow, heavy object is more dangerous than a fast, light one.
lessons.do_now: A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m/s. A 1 kg ball moves at 6 m/s. Which has more kinetic energy? Calculate both and compare. What does this tell you about the importance of speed vs. mass?

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Dynamics carts and track (1 set per group)

engage.description: Show two video clips: (1) A bowling ball rolling slowly toward pins. (2) A tennis ball fired from a machine at high speed. Ask: Which would you rather be hit by? Why? Both can knock things over — what determines how much damage a moving object can do? Introduce kinetic energy as the quantity that captures this idea.

explore.description: Students use dynamics carts with motion sensors. Part 1: Keep mass constant (0.5 kg), vary speed (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 m/s). Calculate KE for each trial. Graph KE vs. v and KE vs. v^2. Part 2: Keep speed constant (1.0 m/s), vary mass (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 kg). Calculate KE and graph KE vs. m. Students identify: KE depends on the square of velocity but linearly on mass.

explain.description: Formalize: KE = 1/2 mv^2. Point out the squared velocity term — doubling speed quadruples KE. This is why highway accidents are so much more dangerous than parking lot accidents. Introduce the work-energy theorem: W_net = delta KE = KE_f - KE_i. If positive net work is done, KE increases (object speeds up). If negative net work is done, KE decreases (object slows down). Work through two examples: (1) A 1200 kg car accelerates from 10 m/s to 25 m/s — find the net work done. (2) A braking force does -8000 J of work on a 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s — find the final speed.

elaborate.description: Application: A 0.145 kg baseball is pitched at 40 m/s toward a batter. The batter hits the ball, and it leaves the bat at 45 m/s in the opposite direction. Use the work-energy theorem to find the net work done on the ball by the bat. Then, if the bat was in contact for 0.5 cm, calculate the average force.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 70 kg sprinter starts from rest and reaches 10 m/s. (a) Calculate the change in kinetic energy. (b) How much net work was done on the sprinter? (c) If the sprinter covered 15 m during this acceleration, what was the average net force?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a KE calculation template with blanks: KE = 1/2 (___ kg)(___ m/s)^2 = ___ J. Include a work-energy theorem summary card: 'Net work = final KE - initial KE. Positive net work = speeds up. Negative net work = slows down.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the dynamics cart exploration and all work-energy theorem problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Derive KE = 1/2 mv^2 from W = Fd and the kinematics equations. Analyze how stopping distance depends on the square of speed and explain the physics behind speed limits in school zones.
differentiation.ell: Use bar diagrams to visually represent KE before and after work is done. Provide bilingual vocabulary cards with visual models. Use color-coded energy bars (red = KE before, blue = KE after, green = work done).
differentiation.iep: Provide a step-by-step problem-solving template for work-energy theorem problems. Allow use of formula card on assessments. Reduce the number of practice problems and focus on single-step KE calculations before multi-step problems.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the physics of car crashes and how kinetic energy relates to vehicle safety. Analyze why speed limits exist in school zones and residential neighborhoods, connecting to community safety. Examine how crash test ratings impact different communities — lower-income families often drive older vehicles with fewer safety features.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'kinetic energy': Doubling the speed of a car quadruples its kinetic energy because___. A truck and a car may move at the same speed, but the truck has more kinetic energy because___. The brakes applied a friction force opposite to the car's motion, so the car's kinetic energy___.

vocabulary.definition: The energy an object possesses due to its motion; KE = 1/2 mv^2, measured in Joules
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy; W_net = KE_f - KE_i
Kinetic energy associated with the linear motion of an object's center of mass
The total work done on an object by all forces combined; determines the change in kinetic energy

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Kinetic Energy — The Energy of Motion
Section 2: KE = 1/2 mv^2 — Why Speed Matters More Than Mass
Section 3: The Work-Energy Theorem — Connecting Force and Energy
Section 4: Applying the Work-Energy Theorem to Real-World Problems

cer.phenomenon: On highways, the speed limit is typically 65 mph (29 m/s), while in school zones it is 20 mph (9 m/s). A 1500 kg car traveling at highway speed needs approximately 60 m to stop, but the same car in a school zone needs only about 6 m. Insurance data shows that pedestrian fatality rates increase dramatically above 30 mph.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the relationship between kinetic energy and speed, I claim that small increases in vehicle speed lead to disproportionately large increases in danger because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the kinetic energy of the 1500 kg car at both speeds. Find the ratio of KE at highway speed to KE at school zone speed. Relate this to the stopping distances provided.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because KE depends on v^2, so the car at ___ m/s has ___ times the KE of the car at ___ m/s, even though the speed is only ___ times greater. This means the brakes must remove ___ times more energy, explaining the ___ times longer stopping distance.

lessons.title: Gravitational and Elastic Potential Energy
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can calculate gravitational potential energy using PE = mgh and elastic potential energy using PE = 1/2 kx^2, and explain how energy is stored in each system.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think of something that stores energy just by its position or shape — a stretched rubber band, a ball on a high shelf, a compressed spring in a toy. What happens when that stored energy is released?
lessons.do_now: A 5 kg bowling ball sits on a shelf 2 m above the floor. Calculate the gravitational potential energy relative to the floor. What happens to this energy if the ball falls? Where does it go?

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Springs of different spring constants (2-3 per group)
Ring stands and clamps for hanging springs

engage.description: Show the bungee jumping cluster from the Regents sampler (Macau Tower, 233 m). Ask: When the jumper stands on the platform, they have zero kinetic energy. When they reach the lowest point, they also have zero kinetic energy. But they moved 200 m. Where did the energy go during the fall, and where is it stored at the bottom? Students brainstorm in pairs.

explore.description: Station 1 — Gravitational PE: Students hold masses at different heights (0.5 m, 1.0 m, 1.5 m, 2.0 m) and calculate PE = mgh for each. They verify that PE depends linearly on height by graphing PE vs. h. Station 2 — Elastic PE: Students hang masses from a spring, measure the stretch (x), and calculate PE = 1/2 kx^2 using the spring constant k (provided on a tag or measured by students). They graph PE vs. x and PE vs. x^2.

explain.description: Define potential energy as stored energy due to position or configuration. Gravitational PE: PE_g = mgh, where h is measured relative to a chosen reference point. The choice of reference point is arbitrary but must be consistent. Elastic PE: PE_s = 1/2 kx^2, where k is the spring constant (N/m) and x is the displacement from equilibrium. Connect to Hooke's Law: F = kx (from Unit 3). Work through examples: (1) A 60 kg bungee jumper on a 233 m platform — calculate PE_g. (2) A spring with k = 200 N/m compressed 0.15 m — calculate PE_s.

elaborate.description: Regents connection: Students solve the bungee jumping sampler question — calculating the change in gravitational PE for a 60 kg jumper riding an elevator from the ground to a 233 m platform. Then they draw an energy bar chart showing PE_g, PE_s, and KE at the platform, during free fall (before cord stretches), and at the lowest point.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A spring with k = 400 N/m is compressed 0.25 m and launches a 0.1 kg ball straight up. (a) Calculate the elastic PE stored in the spring. (b) If all this energy converts to gravitational PE, how high does the ball rise?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a side-by-side comparison chart: Gravitational PE (PE = mgh, depends on height, reference point matters) vs. Elastic PE (PE = 1/2 kx^2, depends on stretch/compression, equilibrium is reference). Include a worked example for each.
differentiation.on_level: Complete both station activities and energy bar chart problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Derive PE_s = 1/2 kx^2 from the area under a Force vs. Displacement graph for a spring. Analyze how gravitational PE changes for objects at very large distances from Earth where g is not constant.
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations at each station — students see and feel the spring stretching and masses being lifted before calculating. Provide bilingual energy vocabulary cards with diagrams showing energy storage.
differentiation.iep: Color-coded formula cards: green for PE_g = mgh, blue for PE_s = 1/2 kx^2. Break the exit ticket into single-variable calculation steps. Provide pre-labeled energy bar chart templates.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how the Inca civilization used gravitational potential energy concepts in their terrace farming system — moving water downhill through precisely engineered channels. Connect to modern hydroelectric power, which converts gravitational PE of water to electrical energy, and discuss how dam construction affects indigenous communities worldwide.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'potential energy': A ball at the top of a hill has maximum gravitational potential energy because___. Both gravitational and elastic PE are forms of stored energy, but they depend on different factors because___. The spring was compressed 0.20 m and has a spring constant of 300 N/m, so the elastic PE stored is___.

vocabulary.definition: Energy stored in a system due to the position or configuration of objects within it
Energy stored due to an object's height above a reference point; PE_g = mgh
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object; PE_s = 1/2 kx^2
A measure of a spring's stiffness in N/m; a larger k means a stiffer spring that requires more force to stretch or compress
The position where potential energy is defined as zero; the choice is arbitrary but must be used consistently

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is Potential Energy? — Energy of Position and Configuration
Section 2: Gravitational Potential Energy — PE = mgh
Section 3: Elastic Potential Energy — PE = 1/2 kx^2 and Hooke's Law
Section 4: Choosing a Reference Point
Section 5: Energy Bar Charts — Visualizing Energy Storage

cer.phenomenon: A 60 kg bungee jumper stands on a platform 233 m above the ground at the Macau Tower. The unstretched bungee cord is 50 m long. The jumper falls 200 m to the lowest point, coming momentarily to rest. At the lowest point, the cord has stretched 150 m beyond its natural length.
cer.claim_starter: Based on energy analysis, I claim that at the lowest point, all of the jumper's original gravitational PE has been converted to elastic PE stored in the bungee cord because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the gravitational PE at the platform (relative to the lowest point). Calculate the elastic PE stored in the cord at maximum stretch using the given stretch distance. Compare the two values.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because at the platform the jumper has ___ J of gravitational PE and zero KE, while at the lowest point the jumper has zero KE and zero gravitational PE (relative to that point), so the ___ J must be stored as ___ in the cord.

lessons.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply the law of conservation of energy to solve problems involving the transformation between kinetic and potential energy in systems without significant friction.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever been on a roller coaster, a swing, or a skateboard ramp? Describe the moment when you felt the fastest. Was it always at the lowest point? Why do you think that is?
lessons.do_now: A 2 kg ball is dropped from 10 m. What is its speed just before hitting the ground? Use conservation of energy, not kinematics equations.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Hot Wheels track with loop (1 per group)

engage.description: Set up a Hot Wheels track with a hill and a loop. Release a car from the top of the hill. Ask: How do we know the car will make it through the loop? What if we release it from a lower point? Students predict the minimum release height needed to complete the loop. Introduce conservation of energy as the tool that lets us make this prediction without knowing anything about forces or acceleration along the curved path.

explore.description: Students set up tracks with a hill and a loop. They release a marble from various heights and record whether it completes the loop. They measure the loop diameter and calculate the minimum height using conservation of energy: mgh = mgh_top + 1/2 mv^2_top. Key insight: mass cancels — the result is independent of mass. Students test with marbles of different sizes to confirm.

explain.description: Formalize the law of conservation of mechanical energy: In the absence of non-conservative forces (friction, air resistance), the total mechanical energy remains constant. KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f. Demonstrate using energy bar charts for three scenarios: (1) Ball dropped from height h — PE converts to KE. (2) Ball launched upward — KE converts to PE. (3) Pendulum — continuous KE/PE exchange. Work through two quantitative problems from the Regents bungee cluster style.

elaborate.description: A 65 kg skier starts from rest at the top of a 40 m hill and slides to the bottom (no friction). (a) Find the speed at the bottom. (b) The skier then goes up a second hill 25 m high. Find the speed at the top of the second hill. (c) What is the maximum height of a hill the skier could clear? Students draw energy bar charts for each position.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 0.5 kg ball on a frictionless track is released from a height of 3.0 m. At the bottom of the track, it enters a vertical loop of radius 0.8 m. (a) What is the ball's speed at the bottom of the loop? (b) What is its speed at the top of the loop?

differentiation.approaching: Provide an energy conservation problem-solving template: Step 1 — Identify initial and final positions. Step 2 — List the energy types at each position (KE, PE_g, PE_s). Step 3 — Write the equation KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f. Step 4 — Substitute and solve. Include pre-drawn energy bar chart templates.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the loop investigation and all conservation of energy problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze what happens when friction IS present: Where does the 'lost' energy go? Calculate the work done by friction using W_friction = KE_f + PE_f - KE_i - PE_i. Design a roller coaster on paper that satisfies given constraints (max speed, loop clearance) using conservation of energy.
differentiation.ell: Use energy bar charts as a visual intermediary before writing equations. Color-code energy types consistently (yellow = KE, blue = PE_g, green = PE_s). Provide sentence frames: 'At position ___, the energy is stored as ___. At position ___, the energy has transformed into ___.'
differentiation.iep: Provide a laminated conservation of energy equation card. Use the bar chart as the primary tool — students fill in bars before writing equations. Break problems into steps: 'First find PE_i, then set equal to KE_f, then solve for v.' Reduce the number of problems.

lessons.crse_connection: Analyze the physics of roller coasters, connecting to the contributions of John Allen, considered the 'dean of roller coaster designers,' and discuss how amusement park physics disproportionately affects communities near theme parks. Examine how energy conservation principles are used in designing sustainable transportation systems in cities around the world.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'conservation of energy': The roller coaster's first hill must be the tallest because___. A ball released from 5 m high on a frictionless track will reach the same height on the other side, but if there is friction it will not because___. At the bottom of the pendulum swing, all potential energy has converted to kinetic energy, so the speed is___.

vocabulary.definition: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another; in a closed system, total energy remains constant
The sum of kinetic energy and potential energy in a system; ME = KE + PE
A force (like gravity) for which the work done is independent of path and depends only on initial and final positions; mechanical energy is conserved when only conservative forces act
A force (like friction) that depends on path and converts mechanical energy to thermal energy; when present, mechanical energy is not conserved
The process of energy changing from one form to another (e.g., PE to KE during a fall)

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: The Law of Conservation of Energy
Section 2: Mechanical Energy — KE + PE = Constant (Without Friction)
Section 3: Energy Bar Charts — A Visual Problem-Solving Tool
Section 4: Solving Conservation of Energy Problems Step by Step
Section 5: When Energy Is Not Conserved — The Role of Friction

cer.topic: Conservation of Energy on a Roller Coaster
cer.phenomenon: A roller coaster car (mass 500 kg with passengers) starts from rest at the top of the first hill (height 45 m). The second hill is 30 m high. The third hill is 38 m high. After the third hill, the track is level, and brakes bring the car to rest over a distance of 25 m. A rider notices they feel fastest at the bottom of the first valley and slowest at the top of the third hill.
cer.claim_starter: Based on conservation of energy, I claim that the rider's observations are correct because the speed at any point depends on...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the speed at the bottom of the first valley, the top of the second hill, the top of the third hill, and determine the braking force needed to stop the car on the level section.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because conservation of energy gives v = sqrt(2g(h_initial - h_point)), so the lowest point (h = 0) gives the ___ speed of ___ m/s, while the highest subsequent point (h = ___ m) gives the ___ speed of ___ m/s.

lessons.title: Energy Transformations and Dissipation
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can trace energy transformations through a system, identify where energy is dissipated as thermal energy, and explain why perpetual motion machines are impossible.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about the energy transformations in your morning routine — your alarm goes off, you turn on a light, eat breakfast, walk to school. How many energy conversions can you count?
lessons.do_now: A bouncy ball is dropped from 2 m. It bounces back to only 1.5 m. Where did the missing energy go? Is energy conserved? Explain the difference between energy conservation and mechanical energy conservation.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer
PS3.D: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

engage.description: Challenge: Can anyone build a machine that runs forever without any energy input? Show images of famous perpetual motion machine designs from history. Students discuss in pairs why each would fail. Reveal: Every machine eventually stops because energy is dissipated as thermal energy through friction, sound, and deformation.

explore.description: Station rotation (3 stations, 4 min each). Station 1 — Bouncing ball: Drop a ball from a measured height 5 times, record the rebound height each time. Calculate the fraction of energy retained per bounce. Station 2 — Hand generator: Crank a generator to light a bulb. Feel the bulb get warm. Trace the energy chain: chemical (food) -> kinetic (arm) -> electrical (generator) -> light + thermal (bulb). Station 3 — Rubber band: Rapidly stretch and un-stretch a thick rubber band 20 times, then touch it to your lip. It is warm — mechanical energy converted to thermal.

explain.description: Formalize energy dissipation: In real systems, mechanical energy is always converted to thermal energy through friction, air resistance, and deformation. Total energy is still conserved (First Law of Thermodynamics), but the useful mechanical energy decreases. Introduce efficiency: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input x 100%. Discuss the energy chain of a car: chemical (gasoline) -> thermal (combustion) -> kinetic (pistons) -> kinetic (wheels), with large losses at each step (typical car: ~25% efficient).

elaborate.description: A bouncy ball dropped from 2.0 m rebounds to 1.6 m. Students calculate: (a) The fraction of mechanical energy retained per bounce. (b) The energy dissipated per bounce for a 0.05 kg ball. (c) The height after 3 bounces. (d) The efficiency of one bounce as a percentage.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A light bulb converts 100 J of electrical energy into 5 J of light and 95 J of thermal energy. (a) What is the efficiency of the bulb? (b) Is energy conserved in this process? (c) Why are LED bulbs considered more efficient?

differentiation.approaching: Provide an energy transformation chain template with arrows and boxes. Students fill in the energy form at each stage. Include an efficiency formula card with a worked example.
differentiation.on_level: Complete all three stations and efficiency calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the efficiency of different power plants (coal, natural gas, nuclear, solar) and create a comparison chart. Analyze why the theoretical maximum efficiency of a heat engine is limited by the Carnot efficiency.
differentiation.ell: Use physical stations as primary learning — students experience energy transformations before abstracting. Provide an energy transformation visual chain with icons (flame, arrow, light bulb, thermometer) and bilingual labels.
differentiation.iep: Pre-label energy transformation charts with some boxes filled in. Reduce station data collection to 3 bounces instead of 5. Provide a calculator walkthrough for efficiency calculations.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how energy efficiency and access are social justice issues. Examine how lower-income communities often pay higher percentages of their income on energy bills and have older, less efficient appliances. Highlight the work of Lisa Jackson, former EPA administrator, in promoting energy efficiency standards that disproportionately benefit underserved communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'energy dissipation': A bouncing ball never returns to its original height because___. Total energy is always conserved in a closed system, but mechanical energy is not because___. The car engine converts only 25% of gasoline's chemical energy to useful kinetic energy, so the remaining 75%___.

vocabulary.definition: The conversion of useful mechanical energy into thermal energy (heat) through friction, air resistance, or deformation
The internal energy of an object due to the random motion of its particles; increased when mechanical energy is dissipated
The ratio of useful energy output to total energy input, expressed as a percentage; always less than 100% for real machines
The conversion of energy from one form to another (e.g., chemical to thermal to kinetic in a car engine)
A hypothetical device that operates indefinitely without an energy source; impossible due to energy dissipation

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Energy Transformations — Tracing Energy Through a System
Section 2: Energy Dissipation — Where Does the Lost Energy Go?
Section 3: Efficiency — Measuring How Well Energy Is Converted
Section 4: Why Perpetual Motion Machines Are Impossible

cer.phenomenon: A standard incandescent light bulb converts approximately 5% of electrical energy to visible light and 95% to thermal energy. A compact fluorescent bulb (CFL) converts about 20% to visible light. An LED bulb converts about 40% to visible light. A household uses 30 light bulbs for an average of 5 hours per day, each consuming 60 W (incandescent), 13 W (CFL), or 8 W (LED) to produce the same amount of light.
cer.claim_starter: Based on efficiency data, I claim that switching from incandescent to LED bulbs significantly reduces energy waste and cost because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the daily energy consumption for each bulb type (in kWh). Calculate the annual cost at $0.15 per kWh. Determine how much energy is wasted as heat for each type.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because LED bulbs use only ___ W compared to ___ W for incandescent, saving ___ kWh per year and $___ annually, while producing the same light output. This is because the LED converts ___% of energy to light compared to only ___% for incandescent.

lessons.title: Power
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can calculate power as the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, and compare the power output of different systems.
lessons.circle_prompt: Two students carry identical backpacks to the same floor of the building. One takes the stairs and arrives in 30 seconds. The other takes the elevator and arrives in 60 seconds. Who did more work? Who was more powerful? What is the difference?
lessons.do_now: A motor does 5000 J of work in 10 seconds. A second motor does 5000 J of work in 25 seconds. Both do the same work. What is different about them? Calculate a quantity that captures this difference.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

engage.description: Compare two cars: both can reach 100 km/h, but a sports car does it in 4 seconds while a minivan takes 12 seconds. Ask: If they reach the same speed and have similar mass, they gain similar kinetic energy. What is the sports car better at? Introduce power as the rate of doing work or transferring energy.

explore.description: Staircase power lab: Students measure their mass (using a bathroom scale), the height of a flight of stairs, and the time it takes to walk up and then run up the stairs. They calculate the work done (W = mgh) and the power output (P = W/t) for each trial. Students compare their walking power to their running power and rank classmates by power output.

explain.description: Define power: P = W/t = Fd/t = Fv. Units: Watts (W) = J/s. 1 horsepower = 746 W. Discuss the difference between energy and power: A 100 W bulb and a 60 W bulb can both emit the same total energy — the 100 W bulb just does it faster. Work through examples: (1) An elevator motor lifts 800 kg a height of 20 m in 30 s — find the power. (2) A cyclist maintains a speed of 8 m/s against a friction force of 40 N — find the power.

elaborate.description: A 1200 kg car accelerates from rest to 30 m/s in 8 seconds. (a) Calculate the kinetic energy gained. (b) Calculate the average power output. (c) Express this in horsepower. (d) If the engine is 25% efficient, how much total chemical energy (from fuel) was used?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A crane lifts a 2000 kg steel beam 15 m in 45 seconds at constant speed. (a) Calculate the work done by the crane. (b) Calculate the power of the crane in watts and horsepower.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a power formula reference card showing P = W/t and P = Fv side by side with unit reminders (W in Joules, t in seconds, P in Watts). Include a step-by-step example for the staircase lab calculation.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the staircase power lab and all practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the power output of various energy sources (human body, car engine, power plant, the Sun) and create a powers-of-ten comparison chart. Calculate the average power output of a sprinter during a 100 m dash using work-energy theorem.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical staircase activity as the primary learning experience. Provide a bilingual vocabulary card with diagrams showing the difference between energy (how much) and power (how fast). Sentence frames for comparisons.
differentiation.iep: Pre-fill the staircase lab data table with column headers and units. Provide a step-by-step calculation guide. Allow use of the formula card on assessments.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how James Watt, a Scottish engineer, defined horsepower to market his steam engine to mine owners. Connect to how the Industrial Revolution transformed labor — and how power generation has always been tied to social power, from coal mines employing child workers in England to modern debates about renewable energy access in developing nations.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'power': Two students may do the same amount of work climbing stairs, but the faster student has more power because___. A 100 W light bulb and a 60 W light bulb both produce light, but the 100 W bulb uses more energy per second because___. The crane lifted the beam 15 m in 45 seconds, so its power output was___.

vocabulary.definition: The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred; P = W/t, measured in Watts
The SI unit of power; 1 W = 1 J/s
A unit of power; 1 hp = 746 W; originally defined by James Watt
A unit of energy (not power) used in electricity billing; 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is Power? — Rate of Doing Work
Section 2: Calculating Power — P = W/t and P = Fv
Section 3: Units of Power — Watts and Horsepower
Section 4: Power in Everyday Life — Appliances, Vehicles, and the Human Body

cer.phenomenon: In the 2009 World Championships, Usain Bolt ran 100 m in 9.58 seconds with a mass of 86 kg. In the same competition, a weightlifter performed a clean and jerk, lifting 200 kg to a height of 2.0 m in 1.5 seconds. Both are considered elite athletes.
cer.claim_starter: Based on power calculations, I claim that the weightlifter actually generates more instantaneous power than Bolt, even though Bolt appears more explosive, because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate Bolt's average kinetic energy at the finish (using v = d/t as an approximation) and his average power output. Calculate the weightlifter's work (W = mgh) and power output.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the weightlifter's power output is approximately ___ W, while Bolt's average power is approximately ___ W. However, Bolt's peak power during the acceleration phase is ___ because ___.

lessons.title: Simple Machines and Mechanical Advantage
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can calculate the ideal mechanical advantage and efficiency of simple machines and explain how machines trade force for distance while conserving energy.
lessons.circle_prompt: What tools or machines do you use regularly that make tasks easier — a ramp for moving heavy objects, a bottle opener, scissors, a pulley? How do they actually help you?
lessons.do_now: A 200 N box must be lifted 1.5 m onto a truck. You could lift it straight up, or push it up a 4.5 m ramp. Calculate the work done in each case (ignoring friction). What does the ramp change, and what stays the same?
materials: Pulleys (single and compound, 1 set per group)

engage.description: Show images of the Egyptian pyramids and ask: How did workers move 2.5-ton stone blocks to a height of 146 m without modern cranes? Display illustrations of ramps, levers, and rollers used in ancient construction. Machines do not reduce the amount of work — they make it possible by reducing the force needed.

explore.description: Groups compare the force needed to lift a 1 kg mass straight up versus pulling it up ramps at different angles. They measure the input force (spring scale reading) and input distance (ramp length) for each angle. Students calculate: Work_input = F_input x d_input and Work_output = F_gravity x height. They compute efficiency = W_out/W_in x 100% and IMA = d_input/d_output for each ramp.

explain.description: Define simple machines: devices that change the direction or magnitude of a force. Ideal Mechanical Advantage (IMA) = distance_input / distance_output. Actual Mechanical Advantage (AMA) = Force_output / Force_input. Efficiency = AMA/IMA x 100% = Work_out/Work_in x 100%. Key principle: a machine cannot multiply energy — it trades force for distance. Briefly overview six simple machines: lever, inclined plane, wedge, screw, wheel and axle, pulley.

elaborate.description: Pulley system challenge: Students set up a single fixed pulley, then a single movable pulley, then a compound pulley system. For each, they measure the force required to lift a 5 N weight and the distance they must pull the rope. They calculate IMA and efficiency for each system and explain the trade-off.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A worker uses a 6 m ramp to push a 300 N crate to a platform 2 m high, applying 120 N of force. (a) Calculate the IMA. (b) Calculate the AMA. (c) Calculate the efficiency. (d) Explain where the 'lost' energy goes.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a simple machines reference card with diagrams of each type and formulas for IMA. Include a side-by-side comparison: 'Without machine: big force, small distance. With machine: small force, big distance. Same work.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the ramp and pulley exploration and all calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Design a compound machine (combination of two or more simple machines) to lift a heavy object from the ground to a table. Calculate the theoretical IMA of the compound system and test it. Research how the Archimedes screw is still used for irrigation in developing countries.
differentiation.ell: Use hands-on exploration as the primary learning tool. Provide labeled diagrams of each simple machine in English and native language. Use consistent symbols in all formulas.
differentiation.iep: Provide a step-by-step efficiency calculation guide with fill-in-the-blank format. Focus on ramp and pulley problems only (skip the other four simple machines for now). Allow partner work on the exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how simple machines have been fundamental to every civilization's development — Archimedes' lever and screw in ancient Greece, the shaduf (lever-based water lift) in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, and the terrace systems of the Inca Empire that used inclined planes to manage water and agriculture across the Andes.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'mechanical advantage': A ramp makes it easier to push a heavy object to a higher elevation because___. A single fixed pulley changes the direction of force but does not reduce the effort, but a movable pulley reduces the effort by half because___. The efficiency of the ramp was only 83%, so___.

vocabulary.definition: A device that changes the magnitude or direction of a force; the six types are lever, inclined plane, wedge, screw, wheel and axle, and pulley
The mechanical advantage of a machine assuming no friction; IMA = distance_input / distance_output
The mechanical advantage measured in a real machine; AMA = force_output / force_input
The ratio of useful work output to total work input for a machine; efficiency = (W_out / W_in) x 100%; always less than 100% due to friction
In simple machines, the exchange between force and distance — reducing the required force always increases the required distance

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is a Simple Machine? — Changing Force, Not Energy
Section 2: Ideal and Actual Mechanical Advantage
Section 3: Efficiency of Machines
Section 4: The Six Simple Machines — Examples and Applications

cer.phenomenon: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built with approximately 2.3 million stone blocks, each weighing about 2,500 kg. The pyramid is 146 m tall. Workers had no powered machinery. Archaeological evidence suggests they used long ramps with a gradual incline of about 7-8 degrees. An alternative theory proposes shorter, steeper ramps with a 20-degree incline wrapped around the pyramid.
cer.claim_starter: Based on mechanical advantage calculations, I claim that the longer, gentler ramp would have required less force per worker but more total distance, while the steeper ramp would require more force but less distance, because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the IMA for each ramp design. Determine the force required to push a 2,500 kg block up each ramp. Estimate the number of workers needed if each can exert approximately 500 N.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the 7-degree ramp has an IMA of approximately ___, requiring only ___ N of force (about ___ workers), while the 20-degree ramp has an IMA of only ___, requiring ___ N (about ___ workers). This illustrates the fundamental trade-off in simple machines.

lessons.title: Energy Conversions and Engineering Design
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can design, build, and refine a device that converts one form of energy to another within given constraints, and explain how to optimize its efficiency.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could invent a device that captures wasted energy from everyday life — body heat, vibrations from walking, sound from a crowded room — what would you create? How would you use the captured energy?
lessons.do_now: A wind turbine converts kinetic energy of moving air into electrical energy. If a turbine receives 500,000 J of wind energy per second and produces 175,000 J of electrical energy per second, what is its efficiency? What happens to the remaining energy?

dci: PS3.D: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

engage.description: Present the Regents sampler problem about a device that converts one form of energy to another (HS-PS3-3). Show the performance level descriptor: at Level 4, students must 'design, build, and refine a device that works within given constraints to convert one form of energy into another form of energy.' Set the challenge: Build a rubber band-powered car that converts elastic PE to kinetic energy and travels the farthest distance.

explore.description: Engineering design challenge: Groups receive identical materials kits and must build a rubber band-powered vehicle that travels as far as possible along the floor. Constraints: must use only provided materials, must fit within a 20 cm x 15 cm footprint, must start from rest. Groups have 10 minutes to build and 5 minutes to test and measure distances. Record initial elastic PE (estimated) and final distance traveled.

explain.description: Class debriefs: Which designs went farthest? Why? Discuss energy transformation chain: elastic PE (rubber band) -> kinetic energy (wheels) -> thermal energy (friction). What design features maximized efficiency? (Less friction, better axle design, optimal rubber band tension.) Connect to HS-PS3-3 PLDs: students must explain how their device could be refined and how a similar device could solve a real-world problem.

elaborate.description: Groups refine their designs based on first-round data. They make one modification, justify it in writing using energy concepts, and test again. They calculate the improvement in distance and efficiency. Students write a brief engineering report: original design, modification made, physics reasoning, results.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (a) Trace the energy transformations in your rubber band car from start to stop. (b) Identify where energy was dissipated. (c) Describe one design change you would make if you had additional materials, and explain why it would improve efficiency using energy concepts.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-made chassis template that students can modify. Include a design checklist: 'Does your car have wheels? Is the rubber band attached securely? Can the wheels spin freely?' Offer an energy transformation chain template to fill in.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the design challenge with one refinement cycle as described.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the theoretical maximum distance using the elastic PE of the rubber band (measure k and x). Compare to actual distance and quantify the energy lost to friction. Propose a design that could achieve 50% or higher efficiency.
differentiation.ell: Provide labeled diagrams of sample car designs. Use hands-on building as primary learning. Pair with a strong English speaker for the written report but allow verbal explanation of design reasoning.
differentiation.iep: Pre-assemble a basic chassis and allow students to focus on the rubber band mechanism. Reduce the written report to sentence starters: 'My car converts ___ energy to ___ energy. I changed ___ because ___.' Provide extra building time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how communities around the world are innovating with energy conversion technologies. Highlight William Kamkwamba, a Malawian inventor who built a windmill from scrap materials at age 14 to generate electricity for his village during a famine. Connect to how engineering design in physics can address real community needs, especially in areas without reliable power infrastructure.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'energy conversion': A rubber band car stores energy as elastic potential energy before release because___. Our first design traveled 3 meters, but after reducing friction on the axles it traveled 4.5 meters because___. The theoretical maximum distance was 6 meters based on stored PE, so our efficiency was approximately___.

vocabulary.definition: A machine or system that transforms energy from one form to another (e.g., solar panel: light to electrical; motor: electrical to kinetic)
A limitation or requirement that a design must satisfy (e.g., material limits, size, cost, safety)
The process of testing, evaluating, and refining a design to improve performance
A sequence showing the forms of energy as it is transformed through a system from input to output, including losses

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Energy Conversion Devices in Everyday Life
Section 2: The Engineering Design Process — Define, Design, Build, Test, Refine
Section 3: Optimizing Efficiency — Reducing Energy Losses
Section 4: Connecting Energy Concepts to Real-World Engineering

cer.phenomenon: A school installs two energy systems: (1) Rooftop solar panels that convert sunlight to electricity at 22% efficiency. (2) A small wind turbine that converts wind kinetic energy to electricity at 35% efficiency. The solar panels receive an average of 5.0 kWh/m^2/day of solar energy and cover 100 m^2. The wind turbine intercepts an average of 800 kWh/day of wind energy.
cer.claim_starter: Based on efficiency and energy input calculations, I claim that the solar panels generate more total electricity despite having lower efficiency because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the daily electrical output of each system using efficiency and energy input data.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the solar panels produce ___ kWh/day while the wind turbine produces ___ kWh/day. Even though the turbine has a higher efficiency (___% vs. ___%), the solar panels receive ___ times more energy input, which demonstrates that both efficiency and energy input matter.

lessons.title: Unit 6 Review and Assessment
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can solve multi-step problems involving work, energy, power, and conservation of energy, connecting these concepts to real-world phenomena.
lessons.circle_prompt: What concept from this unit surprised you the most? Was it that holding a heavy box is not 'work' in physics, that speed matters more than mass for kinetic energy, or something else?
lessons.do_now: Quick review: A 50 kg skateboarder starts from rest at the top of a 6 m halfpipe. Assuming no friction, calculate their speed at the bottom. Then calculate the kinetic energy at the bottom. Then calculate the power if they reached the bottom in 2 seconds.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

engage.description: Kahoot or quick-fire whiteboard review: Display 6 rapid-fire questions covering key formulas and concepts (W = Fd cos theta, KE = 1/2 mv^2, PE = mgh, PE = 1/2 kx^2, conservation of energy, P = W/t). Students hold up whiteboards with answers. Address common errors immediately.

explore.description: Problem carousel: Six stations around the room, each with a multi-step energy problem (Regents-style). Station 1: Work at an angle. Station 2: Work-energy theorem. Station 3: Conservation with gravitational PE. Station 4: Spring-launches and elastic PE. Station 5: Energy bar charts with friction. Station 6: Power calculations. Groups rotate every 2 minutes, solving one problem per station.

explain.description: Teacher reviews the most commonly missed problems from the carousel. Focus on: (1) Remembering to include the angle in work calculations. (2) Setting up conservation of energy equations correctly — identifying what energy forms exist at each position. (3) Understanding when mechanical energy is NOT conserved (friction present). Display student work samples and discuss strategies.

elaborate.description: Regents cluster practice: Students work through a complete bungee jumping-style cluster (5 questions) integrating gravitational PE, kinetic energy, elastic PE, conservation of energy, and energy dissipation. This mirrors the format they will see on the exam.

evaluate.description: Self-assessment: Students rate their confidence (1-4) on each major skill: calculating work, calculating KE, calculating PE, applying conservation of energy, calculating power. They identify their weakest area and write one specific study action they will take before the exam.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a formula sheet organized by topic with example problems. Allow students to use the formula sheet during the carousel. Provide step-by-step solution guides for one problem at each station.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the problem carousel and cluster practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Create their own Regents-style cluster of 5 questions based on a real-world energy scenario of their choice (e.g., skateboarding, ski jumping, catapult). Include calculations for work, KE, PE, conservation, and power.
differentiation.ell: Provide problem sets with visual diagrams for every question. Include a bilingual formula reference. Allow extra time at stations.
differentiation.iep: Reduce carousel to 4 stations (skip the two most complex). Provide a completed energy bar chart example to reference. Allow extended time and calculator use on all problems.

lessons.crse_connection: Review the diverse scientists and cultural connections from the unit: Emilie du Chatelet, the physics of ancient construction, energy justice, and William Kamkwamba. Students reflect on how understanding energy empowers communities and individuals to make informed decisions about resources and technology.
lessons.hochman_activity: Summary writing: Students write a 4-sentence paragraph summarizing the unit using at least 6 vocabulary terms. Sentence 1: Define work and explain how it relates to energy transfer. Sentence 2: Distinguish between kinetic and potential energy. Sentence 3: Explain conservation of energy. Sentence 4: Define power and explain its importance.

vocabulary.definition: The sum of kinetic and potential energy in a system
In the absence of non-conservative forces, the total mechanical energy of a system remains constant
A visual representation showing the amounts of different energy forms (KE, PE_g, PE_s, thermal) at different positions in a system

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Unit 6 Formula Summary and Problem-Solving Strategies
Section 2: Conservation of Energy — Setting Up and Solving Equations
Section 3: Regents Exam Tips for Energy Questions

cer.phenomenon: A 70 kg pole vaulter sprints down a runway at 9.0 m/s, plants a flexible pole into a box, and is launched 5.8 m into the air, clearing the bar and landing on a soft mat 1.0 m above the ground. The pole bends significantly during the vault, storing elastic PE, then straightens, converting it to the vaulter's kinetic and gravitational PE.
cer.claim_starter: Based on energy conservation, I claim that the pole vaulter cannot clear 5.8 m using running speed alone and must rely on the pole's elastic energy storage and the additional push from their arms because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the maximum height the vaulter could reach using only their initial KE (ignore the pole). Compare this to the actual height cleared. Account for the additional energy sources.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because converting all of the vaulter's KE (= ___ J) to gravitational PE gives a maximum height of only ___ m, which is ___ m short of the actual 5.8 m clearance. The additional energy comes from ___ and ___, demonstrating that the pole vault is a complex energy conversion system.

units.title: Thermal Energy & Conservation
units.anchoring_phenomenon: On a hot summer day, a metal park bench feels much hotter than a wooden bench right next to it, even though both have been in the same sunlight for hours. Why do different materials feel different temperatures when they are actually at the same temperature?
essential_questions: What is the difference between temperature and heat, and how are they measured?
How does thermal energy transfer between objects at different temperatures?
How can we use the conservation of energy to predict the final temperature when two objects are combined?
units.crse_theme: Students explore thermal physics through cultural connections — the physics of cooking traditions from around the world (clay tandoor ovens, Korean stone pot bibimbap, Mexican earth ovens), the development of thermodynamics by scientists like James Joule and Sadi Carnot, and how access to heating and cooling technologies is an equity issue in communities experiencing extreme heat and cold.

formative: Exit tickets on specific heat calculations
summative: Investigation: Calorimetry and Conservation of Energy

investigations: Investigation 4: Thermal Energy Transfer in a Calorimetry System

lessons.title: Temperature, Heat, and Thermal Energy
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can distinguish between temperature, heat, and thermal energy, and explain how thermal energy transfers from hot objects to cold objects until equilibrium is reached.
lessons.circle_prompt: What is the coldest you have ever been? What is the hottest? What did you do to warm up or cool down? How does your body know the difference between hot and cold?
lessons.do_now: A cup of hot cocoa at 80 degrees C and a swimming pool at 25 degrees C — which has a higher temperature? Which contains more total thermal energy? Explain why these are different questions.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Beakers (250 mL and 600 mL, 1 set per group)
Hot plate or access to hot water
Temperature vs. Time data recording sheets

engage.description: Touch test: Students touch a metal object and a wooden object that have been sitting in the room. Ask: Which feels colder? Are they actually at different temperatures? Use a thermometer to verify they are the SAME temperature. The paradox: How can two objects at the same temperature feel different? This introduces the difference between temperature and the rate of heat transfer.

explore.description: Experiment: Pour 100 mL of hot water (60 degrees C) and 100 mL of cold water (10 degrees C) into separate Styrofoam cups. Predict the temperature when mixed. Mix them in a larger cup and record the temperature every 30 seconds until stable. Then repeat with 200 mL hot and 100 mL cold. Students observe that the final temperature is NOT always the average — it depends on how much of each.

explain.description: Define key terms: Temperature — a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance. Thermal energy — the TOTAL internal kinetic energy of all particles (depends on temperature, mass, and type of substance). Heat (Q) — the transfer of thermal energy from a higher-temperature object to a lower-temperature object. Heat always flows from hot to cold until thermal equilibrium is reached. Introduce the Kelvin scale: K = C + 273. Clarify: heat is energy IN TRANSIT, not a property of an object.

elaborate.description: Apply to the anchoring phenomenon: The metal bench and wooden bench are the same temperature, but metal conducts heat away from your hand much faster than wood, making it feel hotter (in summer) or colder (in winter). This is about the RATE of heat transfer, not the temperature. Students explain in writing using the correct vocabulary.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (a) A bathtub of warm water at 38 degrees C and a cup of boiling water at 100 degrees C — which has more thermal energy? Explain. (b) Define heat and explain why it is incorrect to say 'an object contains heat.' (c) Convert 25 degrees C to Kelvin.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a comparison chart: Temperature (average KE, measured with thermometer, degrees) vs. Heat (energy transfer, measured in Joules, flows hot to cold) vs. Thermal Energy (total internal KE, depends on mass and temperature). Include visual diagrams.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the mixing experiment and vocabulary development as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the difference between temperature and thermal energy at the molecular level. Explain why gases at extremely low densities (like in outer space) can have very high temperatures but very little thermal energy.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical touch test and mixing experiment as primary learning before vocabulary. Provide a bilingual vocabulary card with particle diagrams. Use arrows to show heat flow direction.
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-labeled diagram showing particles moving at different speeds in hot and cold objects. Simplify the exit ticket to true/false with explanation for one item. Allow verbal response.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how different cultures developed cooking technologies based on intuitive understanding of heat transfer — the underground earth ovens (hangi) of the Maori in New Zealand, the tandoor clay ovens of South Asia, and the Korean dolsot stone pots. Discuss how these traditional cooking methods demonstrate conduction, convection, and radiation principles.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'thermal equilibrium': Heat flows from the hot water to the cold water because___. The metal bench and wooden bench are at the same temperature, but the metal feels hotter because___. When two objects are placed in contact, heat transfers until they reach the same temperature, so we say they have reached___.

vocabulary.definition: A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance; measured in degrees Celsius, Fahrenheit, or Kelvin
The transfer of thermal energy between objects at different temperatures; always flows from higher to lower temperature; measured in Joules
The total internal kinetic energy of all particles in a substance; depends on temperature, mass, and substance type
The state reached when two objects in contact have the same temperature and heat transfer stops
The SI unit of temperature; K = C + 273; absolute zero (0 K) is the temperature at which particle motion is minimal

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Temperature — Average Kinetic Energy of Particles
Section 2: Heat vs. Thermal Energy — What Is the Difference?
Section 3: Heat Transfer — From Hot to Cold Until Equilibrium
Section 4: Temperature Scales — Celsius, Kelvin, and Conversions

cer.phenomenon: A sparkler burns at approximately 1000 degrees C, yet if a tiny spark lands on your hand it does not cause a serious burn. A bathtub of water at only 50 degrees C can cause a severe scald burn within seconds if you step in.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the distinction between temperature and thermal energy, I claim that the bathtub is more dangerous than the sparkler spark because...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the mass and thermal energy of a single spark (very small mass, very high temperature) to the bathtub water (very large mass, moderate temperature). Estimate the thermal energy of each.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because thermal energy depends on both ___ and ___. Although the spark has a higher temperature, its extremely small ___ means it carries very little total ___. The bathtub water, despite a lower temperature, has a much greater ___, transferring far more ___ to your skin.

lessons.title: Specific Heat Capacity and q = mCdeltaT
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can use the equation q = mC(delta T) to calculate the heat gained or lost by a substance and explain why different materials heat up at different rates.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever noticed that a sandy beach burns your feet on a hot day but the ocean water feels cool? Both have been in the same sun all day. Why does sand get so much hotter than water?
lessons.do_now: Equal masses of water and vegetable oil are heated on identical burners for the same amount of time. The oil reaches a much higher temperature. What property of water explains why it heats up more slowly? Use the Physics Reference Table to find the specific heat of water.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

engage.description: Show a thermal image of a parking lot and a lake next to each other at midday — the parking lot glows red/white (very hot) while the lake is blue/green (cool). Then show the same image at midnight — the parking lot is cool but the lake is still relatively warm. Ask: Why does water resist temperature changes while asphalt changes rapidly? Introduce specific heat capacity as the property that explains this.

explore.description: Lab: Groups heat equal masses (100 g) of water, vegetable oil, and sand on identical hot plates for 5 minutes. They record temperature every 30 seconds and plot Temperature vs. Time for all three on the same graph. Students observe that sand heats up fastest and water heats up slowest. They calculate the rate of temperature change for each substance.

explain.description: Define specific heat capacity (C): the amount of heat needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree C. Units: J/(kg·C). Introduce the equation: q = mC(delta T), where q = heat gained or lost, m = mass, C = specific heat, delta T = change in temperature. Water has an unusually high specific heat (4186 J/kg·C) compared to most materials. Work through three examples: (1) How much heat to raise 2 kg of water from 20 to 80 degrees C? (2) A 0.5 kg piece of iron absorbs 5000 J — what is its temperature change? (3) An unknown metal of mass 0.3 kg absorbs 1200 J and rises by 10 degrees C — what is its specific heat?

elaborate.description: Application: Explain why coastal cities have milder climates than inland cities at the same latitude. The ocean's high specific heat moderates temperature swings. Students calculate: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of a 1 m x 1 m x 1 m cube of ocean water by 1 degree C compared to the same volume of granite?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A 0.4 kg aluminum pot (C = 897 J/kg·C) contains 1.5 kg of water (C = 4186 J/kg·C). Both start at 20 degrees C. How much total heat is needed to raise everything to 100 degrees C? (Students must calculate heat for pot and water separately, then add.)

differentiation.approaching: Provide a q = mC(delta T) problem-solving template: Step 1 — Identify m, C, and delta T. Step 2 — Plug in. Step 3 — Calculate. Include a specific heat table from the Reference Table with key values highlighted.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the heating lab and all specific heat calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Design an experiment to determine the specific heat of an unknown metal. Write a procedure, identify variables, and explain how to use q = mC(delta T) to solve for C. Discuss sources of error.
differentiation.ell: Use the hands-on heating lab as primary learning. Provide a bilingual vocabulary card. Use color-coded graphs (blue = water, yellow = oil, brown = sand) with clear labels. Sentence frames for comparisons.
differentiation.iep: Provide a formula card with q = mC(delta T) and all three rearrangements. Break the exit ticket into two separate problems (pot only, water only) and provide the addition step. Allow calculator use.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how water's high specific heat shapes global climate and agriculture. Explore how communities near large bodies of water — from the Great Lakes to coastal West Africa — benefit from the moderating effect of water. Connect to how climate change is causing ocean temperatures to rise, and the disproportionate impact on island nations and coastal communities in the Global South.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'specific heat': Sand heats up faster than water on a sunny day because___. Both the aluminum pot and the water receive the same amount of heat from the stove, but the aluminum changes temperature faster because___. Water has a very high specific heat capacity, so coastal cities experience___.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree Celsius; units are J/(kg·C)
q = mC(delta T), where q is heat in Joules, m is mass in kg, C is specific heat, and delta T is the temperature change in degrees C
The science of measuring the heat exchanged in chemical reactions or physical changes
A measure of how quickly a material transfers heat; metals have high thermal conductivity, insulators have low

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Specific Heat Capacity — Why Different Materials Heat Differently
Section 2: The Heat Equation — q = mC(delta T)
Section 3: Solving for Any Variable — q, m, C, or delta T
Section 4: Water's High Specific Heat — Climate and Everyday Applications

cer.phenomenon: San Francisco, California, and Wichita, Kansas, are at nearly the same latitude (37 degrees N). In July, San Francisco's average high temperature is 20 degrees C, while Wichita's is 34 degrees C. In January, San Francisco's average low is 8 degrees C, while Wichita's is -6 degrees C. San Francisco is next to the Pacific Ocean; Wichita is 1,500 km from any ocean.
cer.claim_starter: Based on water's specific heat capacity, I claim that San Francisco has a more moderate climate than Wichita because...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the specific heat of water (4186 J/kg·C) to soil/rock (~800 J/kg·C). Calculate how much heat is needed to change the temperature of equal masses of each by 1 degree C.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because water requires ___ times more energy per kg per degree than rock, meaning the ocean absorbs and releases heat much more ___ than land. This moderating effect keeps San Francisco's temperature range to only ___ degrees C compared to Wichita's ___ degrees C range.

lessons.title: Phase Changes and Latent Heat
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can interpret a heating curve, identify phase changes, and explain why temperature remains constant during a phase change as energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever watched ice melt in a drink? The drink stays cold for a long time while the ice is melting, but once the ice is gone, the drink warms up quickly. Why does the ice hold the temperature steady?
lessons.do_now: Water boils at 100 degrees C. If you keep heating boiling water, does it get hotter than 100 degrees C? What happens to all the energy you are adding? Sketch what you think a Temperature vs. Time graph would look like.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

engage.description: Show a video of molten iron being poured into a mold. Ask: The iron starts as a solid, becomes liquid when heated to 1538 degrees C, and can become gas at 2862 degrees C. At each transition, something unusual happens to the temperature. Students predict what they think happens to the temperature during a phase change.

explore.description: Lab: Groups start with 100 g of ice at approximately -5 degrees C and heat it steadily on a hot plate. They record the temperature every 30 seconds until the water has been boiling for 2 minutes. Students plot Temperature vs. Time (the heating curve). They observe two flat regions — one at 0 degrees C (ice melting) and one at 100 degrees C (water boiling) — where temperature stops changing despite continuous heating.

explain.description: Interpret the heating curve: five regions — heating ice, melting (flat at 0 C), heating liquid water, boiling (flat at 100 C), heating steam. During phase changes, added energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, NOT increasing temperature. Introduce latent heat: q = mL, where L is the heat of fusion (L_f = 334,000 J/kg for water) or heat of vaporization (L_v = 2,260,000 J/kg for water). Note: L_v is much larger than L_f because vaporization requires completely separating molecules. Work through a complete heating curve calculation: total heat to convert 0.2 kg of ice at -10 C to steam at 110 C.

elaborate.description: Application: Why do burns from steam at 100 degrees C cause more severe injuries than burns from water at 100 degrees C? Students calculate the heat released when 10 g of steam at 100 C condenses on skin vs. 10 g of water at 100 C cooling on skin. The steam releases the latent heat of vaporization IN ADDITION to the heat from cooling.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Given a heating curve for a substance, students (a) identify the melting and boiling points, (b) label each region with the phase, (c) calculate the heat needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 degrees C using q = mL_f.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-labeled heating curve with five regions clearly identified. Include a formula selection guide: 'Temperature changing? Use q = mC(delta T). Phase changing? Use q = mL.' Color-code regions on the heating curve.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the ice heating experiment and all calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the complete energy budget for converting 1 kg of ice at -20 degrees C to steam at 120 degrees C (five separate calculations). Create a stacked bar chart showing what fraction of the total energy goes to each step.
differentiation.ell: Use the hands-on experiment with real-time graphing as primary learning. Provide a bilingual heating curve diagram with phase labels in both languages. Use color-coding for each phase region.
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-drawn heating curve template with axes labeled. Break the multi-step heating curve calculation into separate worksheet sections, one per region. Allow formula card use.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding phase changes has practical applications in communities — from salting roads in winter (lowering the freezing point to prevent ice) to evaporative cooling used in traditional pot-in-pot refrigerators (zeer pots) in Nigeria and other parts of Africa, enabling food preservation in communities without electricity.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'latent heat': Temperature remains constant during a phase change because___. Both melting and boiling require energy input, but boiling requires much more energy per kilogram because___. Steam at 100 degrees C causes more severe burns than water at 100 degrees C, so hospitals treat steam burns as___.

vocabulary.definition: A transition between states of matter (solid, liquid, gas) that occurs at a specific temperature for a given substance
The energy required to change 1 kg of a substance from solid to liquid at its melting point; for water, L_f = 334,000 J/kg
The energy required to change 1 kg of a substance from liquid to gas at its boiling point; for water, L_v = 2,260,000 J/kg
A graph of temperature vs. time for a substance being heated at a constant rate; flat regions indicate phase changes
The heat absorbed or released during a phase change without a change in temperature; calculated using q = mL

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Heating Curves — What They Show and How to Read Them
Section 2: Why Temperature Stays Constant During a Phase Change
Section 3: Heat of Fusion and Heat of Vaporization
Section 4: Calculating Heat for Phase Changes — q = mL

cer.phenomenon: A restaurant worker accidentally spills 50 g of boiling water (100 degrees C) on one hand and 50 g of steam (100 degrees C) on the other hand. The steam burn is significantly more severe, causing second-degree burns, while the water burn is a first-degree burn. Both liquids and gases were at the same initial temperature.
cer.claim_starter: Based on latent heat calculations, I claim that the steam burn is more severe because the steam releases additional energy during condensation that the liquid water does not release, specifically...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the heat released by 50 g of steam condensing at 100 degrees C and then cooling to skin temperature (37 degrees C). Compare to the heat released by 50 g of water cooling from 100 degrees C to 37 degrees C.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the steam releases ___ J during condensation (q = mL_v) PLUS ___ J during cooling (q = mC delta T), for a total of ___ J. The liquid water releases only ___ J during cooling. The steam delivers ___ times more thermal energy to the skin.

lessons.title: Heat Transfer Methods: Conduction, Convection, and Radiation
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can identify and explain the three methods of heat transfer — conduction, convection, and radiation — and provide real-world examples of each.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about how your home stays warm in winter or cool in summer. What materials, devices, or strategies are used? How do you think the heat actually moves?
lessons.do_now: Three scenarios: (1) A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot at the handle. (2) A room warms up when a space heater is placed on the floor. (3) You feel warmth from a campfire across the clearing. What is different about HOW heat travels in each case?

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Metal rods of different materials (copper, aluminum, steel, 1 set per group)
Hot plate or boiling water bath
Convection current demo apparatus (or colored water and clear container with heat source)

engage.description: Demonstration: Hold a metal rod with wax pellets attached at intervals over a flame at one end. Students watch the pellets melt sequentially from the heated end outward. Then show colored dye in water being heated from below — beautiful convection currents become visible. Finally, hold your hand near (not touching) a hot light bulb — you feel warmth through empty air. Three different mechanisms, three ways heat travels.

explore.description: Station rotation (3 stations, 4 min each). Station 1 — Conduction: Place rods of copper, aluminum, and steel into a hot water bath with wax pellets at the ends. Time how long it takes for the wax to melt on each. Rank materials by thermal conductivity. Station 2 — Convection: Observe colored water heated from below in a clear container.
