Draw the circulation pattern. Predict what happens if heated from the side. Station 3 — Radiation: Use a thermometer to measure the temperature at different distances from a heat lamp. Graph temperature vs. distance.

explain.description: Define three methods: Conduction — heat transfer through direct contact between particles; occurs in solids, liquids, and gases; metals are excellent conductors, insulators (wood, plastic, air) are poor conductors. Convection — heat transfer through bulk movement of fluid (liquid or gas); heated fluid rises (less dense), cool fluid sinks (more dense), creating circulation currents. Radiation — heat transfer through electromagnetic waves; requires no medium; how the Sun heats the Earth through the vacuum of space. Discuss insulators and their role in home energy efficiency.

elaborate.description: Application: A thermos bottle (vacuum flask) is designed to minimize ALL three types of heat transfer. Students diagram a thermos and label: double-walled glass (reduces conduction), vacuum between walls (eliminates conduction and convection), silvered surface (reflects radiation). Students explain why each design feature works.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: For each scenario, identify the PRIMARY method of heat transfer and explain your reasoning: (a) A heating vent on the floor warms a room. (b) Your bare feet feel cold on a tile floor. (c) The Earth receives energy from the Sun.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a three-column comparison chart (Conduction/Convection/Radiation) with rows for definition, requires contact?, requires matter?, and two examples. Pre-fill definitions and students add examples.
differentiation.on_level: Complete all three stations and thermos analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research how passive solar home design uses all three heat transfer methods to heat and cool buildings without electricity. Design a house cross-section showing how conduction, convection, and radiation are managed.
differentiation.ell: Use station demonstrations as primary learning — students see and feel heat transfer before abstracting. Provide bilingual comparison chart with diagrams showing particle movement for each method.
differentiation.iep: Provide a visual reference card with one clear example and diagram for each heat transfer method. Simplify exit ticket to matching format (scenario to method) with explanation for one item.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how traditional architecture around the world uses heat transfer principles — thick adobe walls in the American Southwest and North Africa absorb heat during the day and release it at night (conduction and radiation), while Middle Eastern wind towers (badgirs) use convection to cool buildings without electricity. Connect to modern green building design and energy equity.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'conduction, convection, radiation': A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot at the handle because___. Both conduction and convection require matter to transfer heat, but radiation does not because___. Hot air rises and cold air sinks in a room, so a heating vent placed on the floor is more effective than one on the ceiling because___.

vocabulary.definition: Heat transfer through direct contact between particles; occurs best in solids, especially metals
Heat transfer through the bulk movement of a fluid (liquid or gas); driven by density differences caused by temperature
Heat transfer through electromagnetic waves; does not require matter and can occur through a vacuum
A material that resists the flow of heat (low thermal conductivity); examples include wood, plastic, fiberglass, and air
A material that allows heat to flow easily (high thermal conductivity); examples include copper, aluminum, and silver

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Conduction — Heat Transfer Through Direct Contact
Section 2: Convection — Heat Transfer Through Fluid Motion
Section 3: Radiation — Heat Transfer Through Electromagnetic Waves
Section 4: Insulators and Conductors — Controlling Heat Flow

cer.phenomenon: Two identical houses are built side by side. House A has single-pane windows, no attic insulation, and dark-colored roofing. House B has double-pane windows with argon gas between panes, R-38 fiberglass attic insulation, and light-colored roofing. In summer, House A requires 40% more air conditioning energy than House B. In winter, House A requires 50% more heating energy.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the three methods of heat transfer, I claim that House B is more energy efficient because its design features reduce conduction, convection, and radiation losses, specifically...
cer.evidence_source: Identify which heat transfer method each design feature addresses. Explain how double-pane windows, attic insulation, and reflective roofing each reduce thermal energy transfer.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because double-pane windows reduce ___ (the argon gas is a poor conductor and the sealed space prevents ___), attic insulation traps ___ to reduce ___, and light-colored roofing reflects ___ radiation. Together, these features reduce all three pathways for heat to enter or leave the house.

lessons.title: Calorimetry and Conservation of Energy in Thermal Systems
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply conservation of energy to calorimetry problems, calculating the final temperature when two substances at different temperatures are combined in an insulated system.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you drop a hot stone into a bucket of cold water, the stone cools down and the water warms up. Will they ever reach the same temperature? How could you predict what that final temperature will be?
lessons.do_now: A 0.5 kg piece of iron at 200 degrees C is placed in 2.0 kg of water at 20 degrees C. Without calculating, predict: Will the final temperature be closer to 200 or closer to 20? Explain your reasoning using what you know about specific heat.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Calorimeters (Styrofoam cup nesting sets, 1 per group)
Various metal samples (aluminum, copper, iron — known masses)

engage.description: Present the conservation of energy principle applied to thermal systems: in an insulated (closed) system, the heat lost by the hot object equals the heat gained by the cold object. Q_lost = Q_gained. No energy disappears — it just transfers. Show a diagram of a calorimeter and explain why we use insulated cups (to minimize heat loss to the environment).

explore.description: Calorimetry lab: Groups heat a metal sample (known mass, known material) in boiling water to 100 degrees C. They quickly transfer the metal to a calorimeter containing a known mass of room-temperature water. They record the initial water temperature and the final equilibrium temperature. Using Q_lost = Q_gained: m_metal × C_metal × (T_initial,metal - T_final) = m_water × C_water × (T_final - T_initial,water). Students solve for C_metal and compare to the accepted value from the Reference Table.

explain.description: Formalize the calorimetry equation: Q_hot = Q_cold, or m_1 C_1 (T_1 - T_f) = m_2 C_2 (T_f - T_2). Note the sign convention: Q_lost is positive when written as (T_initial - T_final) for the hot object. Work through two examples: (1) 0.3 kg of copper at 150 degrees C is placed in 0.5 kg of water at 22 degrees C — find T_final. (2) An unknown metal of 0.2 kg at 95 degrees C is placed in 0.4 kg of water at 20 degrees C. T_final = 23 degrees C. Find C_metal and identify the metal.

elaborate.description: Error analysis: Students calculate percent error between their experimental specific heat and the accepted value. Class discusses sources of error: heat lost to the cup and air, imprecise temperature readings, water splashing, metal not fully at 100 degrees C. Students suggest improvements to minimize each error.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: 0.8 kg of water at 90 degrees C is mixed with 1.2 kg of water at 10 degrees C in an insulated container. (a) Set up the conservation of energy equation. (b) Solve for the final temperature. (c) Explain why the final temperature is NOT 50 degrees C (the average).

differentiation.approaching: Provide a calorimetry problem-solving template: Step 1 — Write Q_lost = Q_gained. Step 2 — Expand: m_1 C_1 (T_1 - T_f) = m_2 C_2 (T_f - T_2). Step 3 — Plug in known values. Step 4 — Solve for the unknown. Include a worked example alongside.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the calorimetry lab and all practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Design a calorimetry experiment to determine the heat of fusion of ice. Students write a procedure, identify what to measure, and derive the equation needed. Discuss how this technique is used in food science to measure calories in food.
differentiation.ell: Use the hands-on calorimetry lab as primary learning. Provide a step-by-step lab procedure with diagrams. Use a bilingual variable identification guide. Allow partner work on calculations.
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-set-up equation with blanks to fill in for each problem. Focus on water-water mixing problems before introducing metal-water problems. Allow formula card and calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how calorimetry is used in nutrition science — the calorie content of food is measured by burning food samples in a bomb calorimeter and measuring the heat released. Explore how Wilbur Olin Atwater, an American chemist, developed the system for measuring food energy that is still used on nutrition labels today, and discuss food access and nutrition equity in underserved communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'calorimetry': The final temperature when mixing hot and cold water is closer to the temperature of the larger sample because___. Both objects in a calorimeter reach the same final temperature, but the one with more thermal energy loses more heat because___. Our experimental specific heat was 5% higher than the accepted value, so we concluded that___.

vocabulary.definition: The experimental technique of measuring heat transfer by combining substances in an insulated container and recording temperature changes
An insulated device used to measure heat transfer; minimizes heat exchange with the environment
In a closed, insulated system, the heat lost by the hotter object equals the heat gained by the cooler object: Q_lost = Q_gained
The condition reached when all objects in contact are at the same temperature and heat transfer ceases
A measure of the accuracy of an experimental result compared to the accepted value: |experimental - accepted| / accepted x 100%

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Conservation of Energy in Thermal Systems — Q_lost = Q_gained
Section 2: Setting Up Calorimetry Equations
Section 3: Solving for Final Temperature, Specific Heat, or Mass
Section 4: Sources of Error in Calorimetry

cer.phenomenon: A forensic scientist receives a metal artifact and needs to identify the material without damaging it. They heat the 0.250 kg artifact to 98.0 degrees C in boiling water, then place it in a calorimeter containing 0.400 kg of water at 21.0 degrees C. The final temperature of the system is 25.2 degrees C. The specific heats of possible materials are: aluminum (897 J/kg·C), copper (385 J/kg·C), lead (128 J/kg·C), and iron (449 J/kg·C).
cer.claim_starter: Based on the calorimetry data, I claim that the artifact is made of ___ because...
cer.evidence_source: Use Q_lost = Q_gained to calculate the experimental specific heat of the artifact. Compare the result to the known specific heats of the candidate materials.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because Q_gained by water = ___ J and Q_lost by metal = ___ J over a temperature change of ___ degrees C, giving C_metal = ___ J/(kg·C). This value most closely matches ___, which has an accepted specific heat of ___ J/(kg·C), with a percent error of ___.

lessons.title: Entropy and Unit 7 Review
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain that entropy is a measure of disorder in a system and that natural processes tend toward increasing entropy, and apply all Unit 7 concepts to solve problems.
lessons.circle_prompt: Your room naturally gets messy over time — you have to put in effort to clean it up. Does the physical world work the same way? Can you think of anything in nature that spontaneously becomes more organized without energy input?
lessons.do_now: An ice cube melts in a warm room. This is a natural process. The reverse — water spontaneously freezing in a warm room — never happens. Why not? Both processes conserve energy. What additional principle determines which direction processes go?

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer
PS3.D: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

materials: Food coloring and beakers of water (for diffusion demo)

engage.description: Demonstration: Place a single drop of food coloring in a beaker of still water. Students watch it slowly diffuse throughout the entire beaker. Ask: Will the food coloring ever spontaneously gather back into a single drop? Why not? Conservation of energy allows it — but something else prevents it. Introduce entropy as the reason.

explore.description: Students are given 10 coins. They start with all coins heads up (ordered state) and shake the container. After each shake, they count how many are heads and how many are tails. Repeat 20 times. Graph the results. Students observe that the system quickly moves toward ~50/50 and almost never returns to all heads. This models how systems naturally move toward more probable (disordered) states.

explain.description: Introduce the Second Law of Thermodynamics: In any natural process, the total entropy of a system and its surroundings always increases. Entropy is a measure of the number of possible arrangements of a system — more arrangements = higher entropy = more disorder. Heat naturally flows from hot to cold because this increases total entropy. Refrigerators and air conditioners can move heat from cold to hot, but only by doing work and increasing entropy elsewhere. This is why perpetual motion machines are impossible and why no engine can be 100% efficient.

elaborate.description: Unit 7 review: Students work through a set of mixed problems covering q = mC(delta T), q = mL, calorimetry, heating curves, and heat transfer identification. Focus on Regents-style problems that combine multiple concepts.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (a) Explain in your own words why heat flows from hot to cold and not the reverse, using the concept of entropy. (b) Quick calculation: How much total heat is needed to convert 0.1 kg of ice at 0 degrees C to water at 40 degrees C?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a simplified entropy explanation: 'Things naturally spread out and mix. It takes energy to put them back in order.' Focus on the qualitative understanding rather than calculations. For review, provide a formula summary sheet organized by problem type.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the entropy activities and review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the connection between entropy and information theory. Explain Maxwell's Demon thought experiment and why it does not actually violate the Second Law. Calculate the entropy change for a simple heat transfer problem.
differentiation.ell: Use the coin demonstration and food coloring demo as primary learning. Provide visual before/after diagrams for entropy concepts. For review, include diagrams with all problems.
differentiation.iep: Focus entropy understanding on the qualitative level — 'disorder increases naturally.' For review, provide a problem-type identification guide: 'If temperature changes, use q = mC delta T. If phase changes, use q = mL. If two objects mix, use Q_lost = Q_gained.' Allow formula card use.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how the concept of entropy connects to energy sustainability — fossil fuels represent concentrated, low-entropy energy, and burning them disperses energy as waste heat (high entropy). Highlight the work of Eunice Newton Foote, an American scientist who in 1856 was the first to demonstrate that CO2 traps heat, three years before John Tyndall's more famous experiments — connecting thermodynamics to climate science and environmental justice.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'entropy': Food coloring diffuses throughout a glass of water and never spontaneously gathers back together because___. A refrigerator can move heat from cold food to the warm kitchen, but this does not violate the Second Law because___. The total entropy of the universe always increases, so___.

vocabulary.definition: A measure of the disorder or randomness of a system; natural processes tend toward increasing entropy
In any natural process, the total entropy of a system and its surroundings always increases; heat spontaneously flows from hot to cold
In thermodynamics, the number of possible microscopic arrangements of a system; more arrangements = more disorder = higher entropy
A process that cannot spontaneously reverse direction; all real processes are irreversible because they increase total entropy

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Introduction to Entropy — Why Things Tend Toward Disorder
Section 2: The Second Law of Thermodynamics
Section 3: Entropy and the Direction of Natural Processes
Section 4: Unit 7 Review — Key Equations and Problem Types

cer.phenomenon: A power plant burns coal at 600 degrees C to produce steam that drives a turbine, generating electricity. The overall efficiency is about 33% — for every 100 J of chemical energy in coal, only 33 J becomes electrical energy and 67 J is released as waste heat to the environment at around 30 degrees C. Engineers have tried for over a century to improve this efficiency but have never exceeded approximately 60% for any heat engine.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the Second Law of Thermodynamics, I claim that the maximum efficiency of any heat engine is fundamentally limited and can never reach 100% because...
cer.evidence_source: Apply the concept of entropy to explain why waste heat is an inevitable byproduct of converting thermal energy to work. Discuss how the temperature difference between the heat source and the environment limits efficiency.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the Second Law requires that total entropy must ___ in any real process. Converting 100% of heat to work would mean ___ entropy change, which violates ___. The waste heat at ___ degrees C carries the entropy that must be ___ to satisfy the Second Law.

units.title: Waves & Sound
units.anchoring_phenomenon: At a concert, you can hear the bass guitar from behind a pillar, but you cannot see the guitarist. Sound bends around obstacles easily, but light does not seem to. Both are waves — why do they behave so differently?
essential_questions: What are the properties that define and describe waves?
How do waves behave when they encounter boundaries, other waves, or different media?
How does the wave nature of sound explain the phenomena we hear every day?
units.crse_theme: Students explore wave physics through the lens of sound and music across cultures — the physics of instruments from the West African djembe to the Indian sitar to the Caribbean steel drum, how acoustic engineering shapes concert halls and recording studios, and the contributions of scientists like Maryam Mirzakhani (wave equations on surfaces) and Daniel Hale Williams (ultrasound applications in medicine).

formative: Exit tickets on wave calculations (v = f lambda)

investigations: Investigation 5: Determining the Speed of Sound

lessons.title: Wave Types and Properties
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can classify waves as transverse or longitudinal, identify wave properties (wavelength, frequency, period, amplitude), and calculate wave speed using v = f(lambda).
lessons.circle_prompt: What's the loudest sound you have ever heard? Where were you? Did you feel it in your body, or just hear it? What do you think was actually happening in the air to create that sound?
lessons.do_now: A wave on a string has a wavelength of 0.5 m and a frequency of 4 Hz. Sketch two complete wavelengths and calculate the wave speed. If the frequency doubles, what happens to the wavelength (assuming speed stays constant)?
materials: Long ropes or springs (1 per group)
Wave machine or wave demonstration spring

engage.description: Demonstration: Create a transverse wave on a long rope by shaking one end side to side. Then create a longitudinal wave on a Slinky by pushing and pulling one end. Ask: What do these have in common? (Both transfer energy without transferring matter.) What is different? (Direction of vibration vs. direction of travel.) Students identify which type each is.

explore.description: Slinky lab: In pairs, students create transverse waves and longitudinal waves on a Slinky stretched across the floor. They measure wavelength (distance between consecutive crests or compressions) and frequency (count waves passing a point in 10 seconds, divide by 10). They vary the frequency by shaking faster or slower and observe how wavelength changes. Students calculate wave speed v = f(lambda) for each trial.

explain.description: Formalize wave vocabulary: A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy through matter or space. Transverse waves: particles vibrate perpendicular to wave direction (examples: light, string waves, water surface waves). Longitudinal waves: particles vibrate parallel to wave direction (examples: sound, compression waves in a Slinky). Properties: wavelength (lambda) — distance of one complete cycle; frequency (f) — number of cycles per second (Hz); period (T) — time for one complete cycle (T = 1/f); amplitude — maximum displacement from rest position. Wave equation: v = f(lambda). Work through three examples using the Physics Reference Table.

elaborate.description: Application: A radio station broadcasts at 98.5 MHz. All electromagnetic waves travel at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. Calculate the wavelength of this radio wave. Then: A sound wave in air (v = 343 m/s) has a wavelength of 0.77 m. Calculate its frequency. What note does this correspond to? (Approximately A above middle C, 440 Hz.)

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (a) A wave has a period of 0.02 s. Calculate its frequency. (b) If the wave speed is 340 m/s, calculate the wavelength. (c) Is this wave transverse or longitudinal if it is a sound wave? Explain.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a wave vocabulary visual reference card with a labeled diagram showing wavelength, amplitude, crest, trough, and equilibrium. Include the v = f(lambda) triangle (like the F = ma triangle). Provide the relationship T = 1/f on the card.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the Slinky lab and all wave calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the electromagnetic spectrum and create a scale showing frequency, wavelength, and wave speed for different types of EM waves. Explain why all EM waves travel at the same speed in vacuum but sound speed depends on the medium.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical Slinky demonstrations as primary learning. Provide a bilingual wave vocabulary card with labeled diagrams. Use color-coding: red = transverse, blue = longitudinal throughout all materials.
differentiation.iep: Provide a wave property identification guide with visual cues. Break calculations into single-step problems with formula reminders. Allow use of the v = f(lambda) triangle card on assessments.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore the physics of sound and music across cultures — how the West African djembe drum produces deep bass tones through low-frequency vibrations of its goatskin head, how the Indian sitar uses sympathetic strings that resonate without being plucked, and how Caribbean steel drums are tuned by hammering different areas of a steel oil drum to different thicknesses, creating specific notes.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'wave properties': Sound is a longitudinal wave because___. Both transverse and longitudinal waves transfer energy, but they differ in the direction of particle vibration because___. The radio station broadcasts at 98.5 MHz and electromagnetic waves travel at 3 x 10^8 m/s, so the wavelength is___.

vocabulary.definition: A disturbance that transfers energy through matter or space without permanently displacing the medium
A wave in which particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation; examples include light and waves on a string
A wave in which particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation; examples include sound waves
The distance between two consecutive corresponding points on a wave (e.g., crest to crest); measured in meters
The number of complete wave cycles that pass a point per second; measured in Hertz (Hz)
The time for one complete wave cycle; T = 1/f; measured in seconds
The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its rest (equilibrium) position; related to the energy of the wave
The speed at which a wave propagates through a medium; v = f(lambda)

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is a Wave? — Energy Transfer Without Matter Transfer
Section 2: Transverse vs. Longitudinal Waves
Section 3: Wave Properties — Wavelength, Frequency, Period, Amplitude
Section 4: The Wave Equation — v = f(lambda)
Section 5: Calculating Wave Speed, Frequency, and Wavelength

cer.phenomenon: A guitar string is plucked and produces a note with a frequency of 330 Hz. The guitarist then presses the string at the 12th fret, which cuts the vibrating length in half. The new note has a frequency of 660 Hz. When the guitarist plucks the string harder (with more force), the note sounds louder but the pitch does not change.
cer.claim_starter: Based on wave properties, I claim that changing the vibrating length of the string affects the frequency (pitch) while changing the plucking force affects the amplitude (loudness) because...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the frequencies before and after fretting (330 Hz vs. 660 Hz — doubled). Relate the vibrating length to wavelength. Explain why harder plucking increases amplitude but not frequency.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because halving the string length halves the wavelength, and since v = f(lambda) with speed constant, the frequency must ___ to ___. Plucking harder increases the ___ (displacement from rest) without changing the ___ or ___, so the pitch stays the same but the sound is ___.

lessons.title: Wave Behavior: Reflection, Refraction, and Diffraction
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can describe and diagram how waves behave at boundaries — reflecting, refracting, and diffracting — and explain each behavior in terms of wave properties.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever noticed how your voice echoes in a large empty room or a tunnel? Or how you can hear someone around a corner even though you cannot see them? What is happening to the sound waves?
lessons.do_now: A wave in a rope travels to the right and reaches a fixed wall. Sketch what happens to the wave. Now sketch what happens if the rope is attached to a lighter rope (not a wall). What changes?
materials: Ripple tanks (1 per demo or group)
Laser pointer and protractors (for angle of incidence/reflection demo)

engage.description: Play a short audio clip of an echo in a canyon. Then ask: Why can you hear a marching band around a corner of a building, but you cannot see them until they come into view? Sound waves bend around corners (diffraction), but light waves do not noticeably do so. Why? Today we explore how waves behave at boundaries.

explore.description: Ripple tank or Slinky stations: Station 1 — Reflection: Send a wave pulse down a Slinky to a fixed end and observe the inverted reflected pulse. Then to a free end — observe the upright reflected pulse. Station 2 — Refraction: Send waves along a Slinky from thick to thin sections and observe the speed and direction change. Station 3 — Diffraction: In a ripple tank (or using a simulation), observe waves bending around a barrier and spreading through a narrow opening. Students sketch each behavior.

explain.description: Define three wave behaviors at boundaries: Reflection — wave bounces off a surface; angle of incidence = angle of reflection; wave speed and wavelength remain the same; at a fixed boundary the pulse inverts, at a free boundary it does not. Refraction — wave changes speed and direction when entering a new medium; frequency stays constant, wavelength changes. Diffraction — wave bends around obstacles or spreads through openings; most noticeable when the opening/obstacle is similar in size to the wavelength. This explains the anchoring phenomenon: sound wavelengths (meters) are similar to pillar size, so sound diffracts around pillars; light wavelengths (nanometers) are tiny compared to pillars, so light does not noticeably diffract.

elaborate.description: Regents-style application: A wave with a wavelength of 2.0 m approaches a barrier with a 2.5 m opening. Students predict and sketch the wave pattern after passing through. Then the same wave approaches a 20 m opening. Compare the diffraction in each case. Students explain why AM radio (wavelength ~300 m) can be received behind mountains but FM radio (wavelength ~3 m) cannot as easily.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (a) A wave pulse hits a fixed boundary. Sketch the reflected pulse. (b) A wave moves from deep water (fast) to shallow water (slow) at an angle. Does it bend toward or away from the normal? (c) Explain why you can hear music from a room through a doorway even if you cannot see into the room.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a wave behavior summary card with three diagrams: reflection (wave bouncing), refraction (wave bending at boundary), diffraction (wave spreading through gap). Include the key rule for each.
differentiation.on_level: Complete all three stations and boundary behavior problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research total internal reflection — what happens when a wave tries to move from a slow medium to a fast medium at a large enough angle. Connect to fiber optics. Calculate the critical angle for light going from glass (n=1.5) to air (n=1.0).
differentiation.ell: Use ripple tank or simulation visuals as primary learning. Provide labeled diagrams showing incident, reflected, and refracted waves with bilingual labels. Use consistent arrow colors for incident (red) and reflected/refracted (blue) waves.
differentiation.iep: Provide pre-drawn boundary diagrams for students to complete (draw the reflected or refracted wave). Simplify to qualitative questions: 'Does it speed up or slow down? Does it bend toward or away from the normal?' Allow verbal explanations.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how ancient amphitheaters in Greece and Rome were designed using intuitive understanding of wave reflection and diffraction — the Theater of Epidaurus (built ~340 BC) has such perfect acoustics that a whisper on stage can be heard in the back row. Connect to modern acoustic engineering in concert halls, and how acoustic design affects community spaces like houses of worship and public gathering places.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'wave behavior': Sound can be heard around a corner because___. Both sound and light reflect off surfaces, but only sound noticeably diffracts around everyday objects because___. When a wave enters a denser medium it slows down and bends toward the normal, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The bouncing of a wave off a boundary; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The bending of a wave as it passes from one medium to another due to a change in speed; frequency remains constant
The bending of a wave around an obstacle or spreading through an opening; most significant when the opening or obstacle is comparable in size to the wavelength
The angle between an incoming wave and the normal (perpendicular line) to the surface at the point of contact
An imaginary line perpendicular to a surface at the point where a wave strikes; used as the reference for measuring angles of incidence and reflection

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Reflection — Waves Bouncing Off Boundaries
Section 2: Refraction — Waves Changing Speed and Direction
Section 3: Diffraction — Waves Bending Around Obstacles
Section 4: Why Sound and Light Behave Differently at Barriers

cer.phenomenon: AM radio stations can be received clearly in valleys and behind mountains, even hundreds of miles from the transmitter. FM radio stations, broadcasting at higher frequencies, lose signal strength behind hills and buildings and have a much shorter effective range. Both AM and FM are electromagnetic waves traveling at the same speed (3 x 10^8 m/s).
cer.claim_starter: Based on diffraction principles, I claim that AM radio has better reception behind obstacles than FM radio because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the wavelength of a typical AM station (1000 kHz) and a typical FM station (100 MHz). Compare these wavelengths to the size of mountains and buildings.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because AM wavelengths are approximately ___ m, which is comparable to or larger than hills and buildings, so AM waves ___ around these obstacles. FM wavelengths are only about ___ m, much smaller than obstacles, so FM waves do not diffract significantly and create ___ zones behind obstacles.

lessons.title: Interference and the Superposition Principle
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply the superposition principle to determine the result of two waves meeting, distinguishing between constructive and destructive interference.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever been in a room where there is a 'dead spot' where you can barely hear the music, but if you take one step to the side it gets louder? What might be causing that? Have you ever seen two sets of ripples cross each other in a pool?
lessons.do_now: Two wave pulses travel toward each other on a string. Pulse A has an amplitude of +3 cm and Pulse B has an amplitude of +2 cm. Sketch what happens at the moment they overlap. What is the resulting amplitude?
materials: Speakers and tone generators (for beat frequency demo)

engage.description: Noise-canceling headphones: How do they work? Play a tone through a speaker, then play the same tone with inverted phase through a second speaker. Students hear the sound nearly disappear. Explain that the second wave is the exact mirror image of the first — when they combine, they cancel. This is destructive interference.

explore.description: Slinky exploration: Two students send pulses toward each other from opposite ends. Case 1: Both pulses on the same side (constructive interference — the pulses momentarily combine to create a larger amplitude). Case 2: Pulses on opposite sides (destructive interference — the pulses momentarily cancel). Students sketch before, during, and after for each case. Then use a simulation to see continuous wave interference patterns.

explain.description: Define the superposition principle: When two or more waves occupy the same space, the resulting displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements. Constructive interference: waves in phase (crest meets crest), amplitudes add, louder sound or brighter light. Destructive interference: waves out of phase (crest meets trough), amplitudes subtract, quieter sound or dimmer light. Complete cancellation only occurs when amplitudes are equal and waves are exactly 180 degrees out of phase. Work through graphical addition of two waves point-by-point.

elaborate.description: Application: Two speakers play the same 500 Hz tone. A student walks between them and notices alternating loud and quiet spots. Students draw a diagram showing how path length difference creates constructive interference (path difference = n x lambda) and destructive interference (path difference = (n + 0.5) x lambda). Calculate the wavelength needed for the first quiet spot 1 m from the center line.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Two wave pulses approach each other. Pulse A: amplitude +4 cm. Pulse B: amplitude -3 cm. (a) Sketch the resultant at the moment of overlap. (b) What is the resulting amplitude? (c) Is this constructive or destructive interference? (d) After passing through each other, do the pulses change?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a visual superposition guide: 'Same side = add heights (constructive). Opposite sides = subtract heights (destructive).' Include pre-drawn wave pairs for students to add point-by-point with graph paper.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the Slinky exploration and graphical wave addition as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research how noise-canceling headphones work in detail — the microphone, signal processor, and inverted-phase speaker. Explain the limitations (why they work better for low frequencies). Calculate the beat frequency when two tones of 440 Hz and 444 Hz are played simultaneously.
differentiation.ell: Use the Slinky demonstration and simulation as primary learning before graphical addition. Provide visual before/during/after sketches with bilingual labels for constructive and destructive interference.
differentiation.iep: Provide pre-drawn wave graphs on grid paper for students to add amplitudes at marked points. Focus on two-pulse problems before continuous wave interference. Allow partner work on graphical addition.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how interference principles are used in modern technology — noise-canceling headphones, anti-reflective coatings on glasses and camera lenses, and the LIGO gravitational wave detector. Highlight the contributions of Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne, and Barry Barish, who won the 2017 Nobel Prize for detecting gravitational waves using laser interference — and the thousands of international scientists who made it possible.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'interference': When two crests of equal amplitude meet, the resulting amplitude doubles because___. Noise-canceling headphones produce a sound wave that is the mirror image of background noise, but they work better for low frequencies because___. Two wave pulses passed through each other, so after the overlap___.

vocabulary.definition: When two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements
Occurs when waves combine in phase (crest meets crest), resulting in a larger amplitude
Occurs when waves combine out of phase (crest meets trough), resulting in a smaller amplitude or cancellation
A point of zero displacement in a wave pattern; in interference, where destructive interference occurs
A point of maximum displacement in a wave pattern; in interference, where constructive interference occurs

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: The Superposition Principle — Adding Waves Together
Section 2: Constructive Interference — In Phase, Amplitudes Add
Section 3: Destructive Interference — Out of Phase, Amplitudes Subtract
Section 4: Interference Patterns — Nodes and Antinodes

cer.phenomenon: A factory worker uses noise-canceling earmuffs that contain a microphone and a speaker. The microphone detects incoming noise, a processor generates an inverted version of the sound wave, and the speaker plays it into the ear. The worker reports that the earmuffs effectively reduce the drone of machinery (low frequency, ~100 Hz) but do not cancel the sound of a coworker's voice (varied frequencies, 300-3000 Hz).
cer.claim_starter: Based on destructive interference principles, I claim that noise-canceling technology works better for low-frequency, predictable sounds than for high-frequency, variable sounds because...
cer.evidence_source: Consider the wavelength of 100 Hz sound vs. 3000 Hz sound. Discuss the time the processor needs to analyze and invert the wave compared to the period of each frequency.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because low-frequency sounds have ___ wavelengths and ___ periods, giving the processor ___ time to analyze each cycle and generate an accurate inverted wave. High-frequency sounds change ___ rapidly for the processor to create a precise inverted wave, and human speech is ___, making destructive interference incomplete.

lessons.title: Standing Waves and Resonance
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain how standing waves form, identify harmonics and their node/antinode patterns, and describe resonance as the transfer of energy at a natural frequency.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever swung on a swing set and noticed that you have to pump your legs at just the right rhythm to go higher? What happens if you pump at the wrong rhythm? This is connected to a fundamental wave concept.
lessons.do_now: A guitar string vibrates in a standing wave pattern. The string is 0.65 m long and vibrates in its fundamental mode (one half-wavelength). Calculate the wavelength and, given a wave speed of 400 m/s, the frequency of the fundamental note.
materials: String vibrators or oscillating motors (1 per group)

engage.description: Demonstration: Use a string vibrator to create standing waves on a string. Start with the fundamental frequency — students see one large loop. Gradually increase the frequency — at specific frequencies, the string snaps into 2 loops, then 3, then 4. At frequencies between these, the string vibrates chaotically. Ask: Why does the string only form clean patterns at certain frequencies?

explore.description: Groups use string vibrators (or shaking a rope with a partner holding the other end) to produce standing waves. They find the fundamental frequency (1 loop) and the second (2 loops), third (3 loops), and fourth (4 loops) harmonics. For each, they measure the wavelength (two loops = one wavelength for the 2nd harmonic), identify nodes and antinodes, and calculate the frequency using v = f(lambda).

explain.description: Define standing waves: produced when two identical waves travel in opposite directions and interfere. Nodes are points of permanent destructive interference (zero amplitude). Antinodes are points of permanent constructive interference (maximum amplitude). Harmonics: the fundamental (1st harmonic) has wavelength = 2L. The nth harmonic has wavelength = 2L/n and frequency = nf_1. Resonance: when a driving force matches a natural frequency of a system, energy transfer is maximized and amplitude builds dramatically. Examples: pushing a swing, Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse, opera singer shattering a glass.

elaborate.description: A pipe open at both ends is 1.0 m long. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. Students calculate: (a) The fundamental wavelength and frequency. (b) The frequency of the second and third harmonics. (c) Draw the standing wave pattern for each harmonic, labeling nodes and antinodes. (d) Explain why a shorter pipe produces a higher-pitched note.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A string 0.8 m long vibrates at its third harmonic. (a) How many nodes and antinodes are there? (b) What is the wavelength? (c) If the wave speed is 200 m/s, what is the frequency?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a harmonics reference card showing the first four harmonics with diagrams, node/antinode counts, wavelength formulas, and frequency relationships. Use color-coding for nodes (blue dots) and antinodes (red arcs).
differentiation.on_level: Complete the standing wave exploration and all harmonic calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the harmonic series for a pipe closed at one end (only odd harmonics). Compare to an open pipe and explain why a clarinet (closed pipe) sounds different from a flute (open pipe) playing the same note. Calculate the missing harmonics.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical string demonstration as primary learning. Provide visual harmonic patterns with bilingual labels. Use consistent diagrams with node/antinode patterns clearly drawn.
differentiation.iep: Provide pre-drawn standing wave diagrams for students to label nodes and antinodes. Use a simplified formula: 'Fundamental wavelength = 2 x string length.' Build to harmonics gradually. Allow formula card use.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how resonance has shaped music and architecture across cultures. The didgeridoo, an Australian Aboriginal instrument over 1,500 years old, produces its deep drone through standing waves in a long tube — players create different harmonics by changing their lip vibration frequency. Connect to how understanding resonance has improved building safety in earthquake-prone regions, particularly in communities in Japan, Chile, and Turkey.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'standing waves': A guitar string can only vibrate at certain frequencies because___. The fundamental frequency and the second harmonic both exist on the same string, but the second harmonic has twice the frequency because___. The soldiers were told to break step while crossing the bridge, so___.

vocabulary.definition: A wave pattern that appears to be stationary, formed by the interference of two identical waves traveling in opposite directions
A point on a standing wave that remains at zero displacement; the result of permanent destructive interference
A point on a standing wave with maximum displacement; the result of permanent constructive interference
The lowest frequency at which a standing wave can form; also called the first harmonic; for a string, wavelength = 2L
A standing wave pattern at an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency; the nth harmonic has frequency n times the fundamental
The dramatic increase in amplitude when a driving force matches a natural frequency of a system

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Standing Waves — How They Form
Section 2: Nodes and Antinodes — Fixed Points in the Pattern
Section 3: Harmonics — The Fundamental and Its Multiples
Section 4: Resonance — When Frequency Matching Amplifies Energy

cer.phenomenon: On November 7, 1940, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State collapsed just four months after opening. Wind at only 68 km/h (not unusually strong) caused the bridge to oscillate with increasing amplitude until it tore apart. Engineers later determined that the wind created vortices that matched the bridge's natural frequency of oscillation. Modern suspension bridges are designed with damping systems to prevent this.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the concept of resonance, I claim that the Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed not because the wind was too strong, but because...
cer.evidence_source: Explain how the wind frequency matched the bridge's natural frequency, causing energy to accumulate in the oscillation. Describe what resonance means in terms of energy transfer.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because when the driving frequency (wind vortices) matched the bridge's ___ frequency, each cycle of wind added ___ to the oscillation without allowing energy to dissipate. Over time, the amplitude ___ beyond the structural limits. Modern bridges prevent this by adding ___, which removes energy from oscillations.

lessons.title: Sound Waves and the Doppler Effect
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can describe sound as a longitudinal mechanical wave, explain the Doppler effect, and calculate observed frequency when a source or observer is moving.
lessons.circle_prompt: You are standing on a sidewalk and an ambulance approaches with its siren on. What happens to the pitch of the siren as it passes you? Does the siren itself change, or does your perception change? Why?
lessons.do_now: A tuning fork vibrates at 440 Hz. The speed of sound in air at room temperature is 343 m/s. Calculate the wavelength of this sound wave. Would this same tuning fork produce the same frequency in water? The same wavelength? The same speed?
materials: Tuning forks (various frequencies, 1 set per demo)
Buzzer on a string (for Doppler demo)

engage.description: Demonstration: Attach a buzzer to a string and swing it in a circle. Students clearly hear the pitch rise as the buzzer approaches and drop as it recedes. Ask: Is the buzzer changing its frequency? (No.) What is changing? Introduce the Doppler effect as the apparent change in frequency due to relative motion between source and observer.

explore.description: Activity 1: Students use a tuning fork and a resonance tube partially filled with water. They adjust the water level to find the first resonance point (standing wave in the tube). They measure the tube length and calculate the wavelength (lambda = 4L for the first resonance of a closed tube). Using v = f(lambda), they determine the speed of sound. Activity 2: Using a simulation, students observe wave fronts from a stationary source and a moving source, noting how the wavelengths compress ahead and stretch behind the moving source.

explain.description: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave — compressions and rarefactions in a medium. Speed depends on the medium: ~343 m/s in air at 20 C, ~1480 m/s in water, ~5100 m/s in steel. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. Pitch = frequency (higher frequency = higher pitch). Loudness = amplitude (larger amplitude = louder). The Doppler effect: when a source approaches, wave fronts are compressed (shorter wavelength, higher frequency, higher pitch). When receding, wave fronts are stretched (longer wavelength, lower frequency, lower pitch). Qualitative Doppler relationship from the Reference Table. Discuss applications: radar speed guns, medical ultrasound, astronomical redshift.

elaborate.description: Application: An ambulance siren produces a 700 Hz tone. As it approaches at 30 m/s toward a stationary observer (speed of sound = 343 m/s), students use the Doppler formula to calculate the observed frequency. Then they calculate the observed frequency as the ambulance moves away at 30 m/s. They find the difference in perceived pitch and connect to their everyday experience.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (a) Explain why sound travels faster in steel than in air. (b) A train horn has a frequency of 500 Hz. The train approaches you at 25 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. Is the frequency you hear higher or lower than 500 Hz? Explain using the Doppler effect. (c) Why can't sound travel through outer space?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a sound properties summary card: Speed depends on medium (solid > liquid > gas). Pitch = frequency. Loudness = amplitude. Doppler: approaching = higher pitch, receding = lower pitch. Include a visual diagram of compressed and stretched wave fronts.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the resonance tube lab and Doppler effect activities as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the sonic boom — what happens when a source exceeds the speed of sound. Explain the Mach cone and calculate the Mach angle for a jet flying at Mach 2. Discuss how redshift in astronomy reveals the expansion of the universe.
differentiation.ell: Use the buzzer-on-a-string demonstration and simulation as primary learning. Provide bilingual Doppler effect diagrams with arrows showing source motion and wave compression/stretching. Sentence frames for cause-effect explanations.
differentiation.iep: Focus on qualitative Doppler understanding (approaching = higher pitch, receding = lower pitch) before calculations. Provide a step-by-step Doppler formula guide. Allow use of reference cards on assessments.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how the Doppler effect revolutionized our understanding of the universe — Edwin Hubble used the redshift of galaxies to show the universe is expanding. Also highlight the contributions of Vera Rubin, an American astronomer who used Doppler shifts of stars in galaxies to discover evidence for dark matter, fundamentally changing our understanding of the cosmos despite facing significant gender discrimination in her career.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'Doppler effect': The pitch of an ambulance siren sounds higher as it approaches because___. Sound and light both exhibit the Doppler effect, but we notice it more with sound because___. Distant galaxies show a redshift in their light spectra, so astronomers concluded that___.

vocabulary.definition: A longitudinal mechanical wave caused by vibrations in a medium; consists of compressions and rarefactions
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are close together; corresponds to high pressure
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are spread apart; corresponds to low pressure
The apparent change in frequency of a wave when the source or observer is moving; approaching = higher frequency, receding = lower frequency
The perceived highness or lowness of a sound; determined by the frequency of the sound wave
The perceived volume of a sound; determined by the amplitude of the sound wave

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Sound as a Longitudinal Mechanical Wave
Section 2: Speed of Sound in Different Media
Section 3: Pitch, Loudness, and the Human Ear
Section 4: The Doppler Effect — Why Moving Sources Sound Different
Section 5: Applications of the Doppler Effect

cer.phenomenon: A police officer uses a radar speed gun that emits radio waves at a frequency of 24.150 GHz toward an approaching car. The reflected waves return at a higher frequency of 24.154 GHz. The officer uses this frequency shift to calculate the car's speed. Meanwhile, the driver of the car hears the police siren's pitch change as the police car passes by at an intersection.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the Doppler effect, I claim that both the radar frequency shift and the siren pitch change are caused by the same physical principle applied to different types of waves because...
cer.evidence_source: Explain how relative motion between source and observer causes the radar frequency to increase (car approaching) and the siren pitch to decrease (car receding). Compare the Doppler effect for electromagnetic waves (radar) and mechanical waves (sound).
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because in both cases, relative motion between source and observer causes the observed frequency to ___ when approaching and ___ when receding. The radar gun detects a frequency increase of ___ GHz because the car acts as a moving ___ that reflects the wave back at a ___ frequency.

lessons.title: Digital vs. Analog Signals and Unit 8 Review
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can compare advantages and disadvantages of digital and analog signal transmission, and apply all wave concepts to solve Regents-style problems.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about all the ways information reaches you — your phone, streaming music, Wi-Fi, radio, Bluetooth. How do invisible waves carry so much data? What is the difference between an old vinyl record and a digital music file?
lessons.do_now: A radio station broadcasts at 101.5 MHz. Calculate the wavelength. Is this an analog or digital signal? What are the advantages of each? How does your phone convert your voice into a signal that can be transmitted wirelessly?
materials: Analog and digital signal demonstration (oscilloscope or simulation)

engage.description: Play the same song from a vinyl record (analog) and a digital file. Ask: Can you hear a difference? Show an oscilloscope view of both signals — the analog signal is a continuous wave, the digital signal is a series of discrete samples (staircase pattern). Discuss: When you zoom in enough, a digital signal looks like steps. So why has digital almost entirely replaced analog in modern technology?

explore.description: Activity: Students receive a 'message' encoded in two ways — as a hand-drawn analog waveform on paper and as a series of binary values (0s and 1s). They must try to copy each message by hand. After copying, they compare their copies to the original. The analog copy has accumulated distortion (like a game of telephone), while the digital copy is perfect (0s and 1s are easy to distinguish even with noise). This demonstrates why digital transmission is more reliable.

explain.description: Analog signals are continuous and carry information as variations in amplitude or frequency. Digital signals encode information as discrete binary values (0 and 1). Advantages of digital: noise resistance (easy to regenerate perfect copies), compression, encryption, error correction. Advantages of analog: continuous representation (no sampling artifacts), simpler technology, no conversion needed for natural signals. Discuss sampling rate: higher sampling rate = better digital reproduction of the original analog signal. Connect to HS-PS4-2 PLD: students must evaluate advantages and disadvantages of digital transmission.

elaborate.description: Unit 8 review: Students work through a mixed problem set covering wave equation (v = f lambda), wave behavior (reflection, refraction, diffraction), interference (constructive and destructive), standing waves (harmonics), Doppler effect, and digital vs. analog signal comparison. Focus on Regents-style questions.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (a) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using digital signals for music transmission. (b) Review: A wave has a frequency of 200 Hz and a wavelength of 1.7 m. What is its speed? Is this likely a sound wave in air? Explain.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a digital vs. analog comparison chart with two columns and rows for: signal type (continuous/discrete), noise resistance, copying quality, examples. Include a unit review formula sheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the signal copying activity and review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research how data compression works (MP3, JPEG) and explain the trade-off between file size and quality in terms of sampling and bit depth. Calculate the data rate for CD-quality audio (44,100 samples/second x 16 bits x 2 channels).
differentiation.ell: Use the physical signal-copying demonstration as primary learning. Provide visual comparison diagrams of analog (smooth wave) and digital (stepped wave) signals with bilingual labels.
differentiation.iep: Focus on the qualitative comparison of analog vs. digital. For review, provide a topic-by-topic problem guide with one example and one practice problem per concept. Allow formula card and calculator use.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how the digital divide — unequal access to digital technology and high-speed internet — affects communities, particularly in rural areas and lower-income urban neighborhoods. Highlight how the physics of wave transmission (fiber optics, wireless signals) determines what infrastructure is needed and why some communities are left behind. Connect to current efforts to expand broadband access as a matter of equity.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'digital signals': Digital signals can be transmitted over long distances without losing quality because___. Vinyl records produce a continuous analog signal that some audiophiles prefer, but most consumers use digital music because___. The digital divide disproportionately affects rural communities, so government programs to expand broadband access are___.

vocabulary.definition: A continuous signal that varies smoothly over time; represents information as variations in amplitude, frequency, or phase
A signal that uses discrete values (typically binary: 0 and 1) to encode information; can be perfectly copied and transmitted with high noise resistance
The number of times per second an analog signal is measured to create a digital representation; higher rates produce more accurate digital copies
Unwanted random variations in a signal; digital signals are more resistant to noise because the discrete values (0 and 1) can be distinguished even with some distortion

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Analog vs. Digital Signals — How Information Is Encoded
Section 2: Advantages and Disadvantages of Each
Section 3: How Digital Signals Resist Noise
Section 4: Unit 8 Review — Wave Properties, Behavior, and Applications

cer.phenomenon: A music producer records a concert using both a high-quality analog tape recorder and a digital recorder at CD quality (44,100 Hz sampling rate, 16-bit depth). The analog recording sounds warm and rich on first playback. After making 10 copies of the analog tape (each copy from the previous copy), the quality degrades significantly with audible hiss and distortion. After copying the digital file 10 times, the quality is identical to the original.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the properties of analog and digital signals, I claim that digital recording is superior for preservation and distribution, while analog has advantages for initial capture fidelity, because...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the copying fidelity of each format. Explain why analog copying introduces cumulative noise while digital copying does not. Consider the trade-off of the 44,100 Hz sampling rate.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because analog signals carry ___ variation that degrades each time it is copied (each copy adds ___), while digital signals encode information as ___ that can be perfectly reproduced. However, the original analog recording may capture subtle sound details that fall between the ___ samples per second of the digital recorder.

units.anchoring_phenomenon: The passenger side mirror on a car carries the warning 'Objects in mirror are closer than they appear.' The rearview mirror inside the car does not have this warning. Both are mirrors — why do they show objects differently, and how does the shape of a mirror determine what image you see?

How do mirrors and lenses manipulate light to serve practical purposes?
What is the electromagnetic spectrum and how does photon energy relate to frequency?

lessons.title: Law of Reflection and Plane Mirrors
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply the law of reflection to predict the path of light rays and locate the image formed by a plane mirror.
lessons.circle_prompt: Share something you have seen that glows, reflects, or bends light in an interesting way — a rainbow, sunlight through a window, your reflection in a puddle, a laser show. What caught your attention about it?
lessons.do_now: You stand 2 m in front of a flat mirror. Where does your image appear to be? Is it in front of or behind the mirror? Is it the same size as you? Is it right-side up or upside down?

engage.description: Show the automotive optics Regents sampler — the rearview mirror diagram. A plane mirror forms a virtual image that appears behind the mirror. Ask: How does light from an object behind the car reach the driver's eye? Students trace a possible light path. Introduce the law of reflection as the rule governing how light bounces off surfaces.

explore.description: Lab: Students shine a laser or ray from a ray box at a plane mirror at various angles. They use a protractor to measure the angle of incidence (between the incoming ray and the normal) and the angle of reflection (between the reflected ray and the normal). They record 5 pairs of angles and discover the law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection. Then they use two mirrors at right angles and trace what happens to a ray that bounces between them.

explain.description: Formalize the law of reflection: theta_i = theta_r, measured from the normal. For plane mirrors: the image is virtual (light does not actually pass through it), located the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, the same size as the object, and laterally inverted (left-right reversed). Demonstrate image location using ray diagrams: draw two rays from the object to the mirror, reflect them using the law of reflection, and extend the reflected rays behind the mirror to find where they appear to intersect (the image location). Connect to the Regents sampler question about constructing the incident ray for a rearview mirror.

elaborate.description: Application: A 1.7 m tall person stands 3.0 m from a plane mirror. Students draw the ray diagram to locate the image. Then: What is the minimum mirror height needed for the person to see their full body? Students discover through geometric reasoning that the mirror must be at least half the person's height, regardless of the distance.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (a) A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of 35 degrees to the surface. What is the angle of incidence? What is the angle of reflection? (b) Describe four characteristics of the image formed by a plane mirror (location, size, orientation, type).

differentiation.approaching: Provide a step-by-step ray diagram guide with pre-drawn mirror and normal line. Include a reminder: angles are measured from the NORMAL, not the surface. Provide a plane mirror image characteristics card.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the reflection measurement lab and ray diagram exercises as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Solve the problem of two plane mirrors at an angle: If two mirrors are placed at 60 degrees to each other, how many images of an object placed between them are formed? Derive the formula: number of images = (360/angle) - 1. Test with mirrors.
differentiation.ell: Use the laser/mirror demonstration as primary learning. Provide labeled ray diagrams with bilingual terms (angle of incidence, angle of reflection, normal line). Use consistent arrow colors for incident (red) and reflected (blue) rays.
differentiation.iep: Provide pre-drawn diagrams with the mirror and normal already in place. Students only need to draw the reflected ray using a protractor. Simplify image characteristics to a checklist format.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen), an 11th-century Iraqi scientist considered the father of modern optics. His Book of Optics (1011-1021 CE) was the first to correctly explain that vision occurs when light reflects off objects and enters the eye (not the other way around, as the Greeks believed). His work on reflection, refraction, and the camera obscura influenced European scientists for centuries.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'reflection': The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection because___. Your image in a plane mirror appears to be behind the mirror, but no light actually passes through the mirror because___. Two plane mirrors were placed at right angles to each other, so a ray entering from any direction___.

vocabulary.definition: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, with both angles measured from the normal to the surface
An imaginary line drawn perpendicular to a reflecting or refracting surface at the point where light strikes it
An image formed where reflected or refracted rays appear to converge when extended backward; cannot be projected on a screen
A flat reflecting surface that produces a virtual, upright, same-size image at equal distance behind the mirror
The angle between the incoming ray and the normal at the point of contact

Section 2: Plane Mirror Images — Virtual, Upright, Same Size
Section 3: Drawing Ray Diagrams for Plane Mirrors
Section 4: Applications of Plane Mirror Reflection

cer.phenomenon: In the Regents automotive optics sampler, students examine three types of mirrors on a car: the rearview mirror (plane/flat), the driver's side mirror (plane/flat), and the passenger side mirror (convex/curved outward). The rearview and driver's side mirrors show objects at their actual size, but the passenger side mirror shows objects smaller than they really are. Only the passenger side mirror carries the warning 'Objects in mirror are closer than they appear.'
cer.claim_starter: Based on the law of reflection and mirror geometry, I claim that the convex passenger mirror makes objects appear smaller and farther away because...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the image characteristics of a plane mirror (same size, same distance) to a convex mirror (smaller, appears farther). Explain how the curved surface reflects light differently than a flat surface.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because a convex mirror reflects light rays ___ (diverging), making the image appear ___ and ___ than the object. This design gives the driver a ___ field of view, but the trade-off is that objects appear ___, creating a safety concern that requires the warning label.

lessons.title: Curved Mirrors — Concave and Convex
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can draw ray diagrams for concave and convex mirrors, describe the images formed at various object positions, and use the mirror equation to calculate image distance and magnification.
lessons.circle_prompt: Where have you seen curved mirrors in everyday life — a makeup mirror, a security mirror in a store, a car headlight, a satellite dish? What do these curved surfaces do differently than a flat mirror?
lessons.do_now: A concave mirror has a focal length of 15 cm. An object is placed 30 cm from the mirror. Using the mirror equation (1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i), find the image distance. Is the image real or virtual?
materials: Ray diagram worksheets with pre-drawn mirrors

engage.description: Show the Regents automotive optics sampler diagram of a car headlight. The concave mirror behind the bulb focuses light into a parallel beam. Ask: Why is the bulb placed at the focal point? What would happen if it were at a different position? Students predict before investigation.

explore.description: Concave mirror investigation: Students place a small light source at different positions relative to a concave mirror and use a white screen to find where a clear image forms. Position 1: Object far away (beyond C) — find the image. Position 2: Object at C — find the image. Position 3: Object between C and F. Position 4: Object inside F — no real image on screen (the image is virtual). Students record object distance, image distance, and image characteristics (size, orientation) for each position.

explain.description: Teach the three principal rays for curved mirrors: (1) Parallel ray reflects through the focal point. (2) Ray through the focal point reflects parallel. (3) Ray through the center of curvature reflects back on itself. For concave mirrors: images depend on object position — real/inverted when beyond F, virtual/upright when inside F. For convex mirrors: images are always virtual, upright, and reduced. Introduce the mirror equation: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i. Magnification: M = h_i/h_o = -d_i/d_o. Sign conventions: real image d_i positive, virtual image d_i negative. Concave f positive, convex f negative.

elaborate.description: Students solve the Regents sampler problems: (1) Using the convex mirror data from the automotive optics cluster (object height 16 cm, object distance 240 cm, image height 2.5 cm, image distance from Table 1 for Trial 1), calculate the missing image distance using the mirror equation. (2) Draw a ray diagram for a convex mirror from the sampler showing the object at two different distances and verify the image characteristics change as described.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: An object is placed 20 cm from a concave mirror with focal length 10 cm. (a) Use the mirror equation to find the image distance. (b) Calculate the magnification. (c) Is the image real or virtual? Upright or inverted? Larger or smaller?

differentiation.approaching: Provide ray diagram templates with pre-drawn concave and convex mirrors, principal axis, focal point, and center of curvature. Include a step-by-step guide for the three principal rays. Provide a mirror equation rearrangement card.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the concave mirror investigation and all ray diagram and mirror equation problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Derive the mirror equation from geometric principles using similar triangles. Calculate the focal length of a concave mirror needed to project an image of a specific size at a specific distance (like a projector design problem).
differentiation.ell: Use the physical mirror and light source experiment as primary learning before ray diagrams. Provide ray diagram templates with bilingual labels. Use color-coding for the three principal rays (red, blue, green).
differentiation.iep: Provide pre-drawn ray diagrams with two of three rays already drawn; students draw the third and locate the image. Break the mirror equation into calculator steps. Provide a sign convention reference card.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how curved mirrors are essential to modern technology — from satellite dishes and solar concentrators to the Hubble Space Telescope's primary mirror. Highlight the James Webb Space Telescope's gold-plated beryllium mirrors designed to capture infrared light from the earliest galaxies, and the international collaboration of scientists and engineers from 14 countries who built it.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'curved mirrors': A headlight uses a concave mirror with the bulb at the focal point because___. Both concave and convex mirrors reflect light, but they form different types of images because___. The passenger side mirror on a car is convex, so objects appear___.

vocabulary.definition: A curved mirror that converges light; the reflecting surface curves inward like a bowl
A curved mirror that diverges light; the reflecting surface curves outward; always produces virtual, upright, reduced images
The point where parallel rays converge (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex) after reflecting from a curved mirror
The center of the sphere from which the curved mirror is a section; located at twice the focal length from the mirror
1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i, relating the focal length, object distance, and image distance for curved mirrors
The ratio of image height to object height; M = h_i/h_o = -d_i/d_o; positive M = upright image, negative M = inverted image
An image formed where light rays actually converge; can be projected on a screen; d_i is positive
